sections.heading: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Collection of connective tissue under skin, divided into superficial, deep & internal fasciae.

sections.heading: Superficial Fascia vs Deep Fascia
sections.text:
| Superficial Fascia | Deep Fascia
Nature | Loose connective tissue immediately deep to skin allowing skin to move freely on underlying structures. | Inelastic membrane of compact & regular collagen fibers.
Distribution | Contains variable quantity of fat more in females.
• Fat is abundant in breast, ant. abdominal wall & gluteal region,
• less in limbs
• absent in eyelid, penis & scrotum | Well defined in limbs, very strong in palm & sole, absent in face and anterior abdominal wall
Functions | 1-Softens and smoothens body surface.
2-Facitilates skin movement on underlying structures.
3-Prevents heat loss (thermal insulator).
4-Conducting medium for nerves, blood vessels and lymphatics supplying the skin.
5-Contains muscles; in face (expression muscles).
6-Contains glands; mammary gland. | 1-Formation of broad sheets: Surround different groups of muscles, so fix underlying structures in position, give attachment to some muscles & help venous return.
2-Formation of intermuscular septa & interosseous membranes: Separate different groups of muscles with different actions & nerve supply. Also increase surface area for muscle attachment.
3-Formation of retinacula: Thickened localized transverse bands at wrist & ankle to keep tendons in position .
4-Formation of palmar & planter aponeurosis: Thick strong layers to protect vessels, nerves & tendons.
5-Formation of fibrous sheaths around big vessels: Carotid sheath around carotid arteries, internal jugular vein & vagus nerve (in neck).

sections.heading: CLINICAL IMPORTANCE:
sections.text:
• Knowledge of deep fascia arrangement help to explain infection path when spreading from primary site (infection can spread from mouth floor to larynx).
• Fluid accumulation in superficial fascia leads to edema.
• Skin mobilization after its incision occurs at superficial fascia plane & skin incision along skin crease heals with minimal scar.

sections.heading: a) BONES — DEFINITION:
sections.text: Hard type of connective tissue forming skeleton.

sections.heading: a) BONES — FUNCTIONS:
sections.text:
1-Give specific shape & provides central axis.
2-Protect vital organs; skull protects brain, thoracic cage protects heart & lungs.
3-Surface area for muscle attachment & form joints (important part of locomotor system).
4-Support & transmit body weight; vertebral column to bony pelvis, lower limbs, feet & ground.
5-Form blood elements in bone marrow & store calcium.

sections.heading: a) BONES — CLASSIFICATION: A) According to position in body;
sections.text:
*Axial skeleton: Skull, mandible, hyoid, sternum, ribs & vertebral column.
*Appendicular (peripheral )skeleton: Bones of upper & lower limbs.

sections.heading: a) BONES — CLASSIFICATION: B) According to ossification process (process of bone formation);
sections.text:
*Intra-membranous ossification: Bones develop directly from connective tissue membrane (mesenchyme). Examples: Skull cap & clavicle. It occurs at one or more ossification sites.
*Intra-cartilaginous ossification: Connective tissue membrane (mesenchyme) is changed into cartilage which dissolves & disappears to be replaced by bones.
Examples: Skull base, long bones, ribs & vertebrae.

sections.heading: c) According to shape; (Long / Short / Flat / Irregular / Pneumatic / Sesamoid)
sections.text:
Type | Book text
LONG BONES (Long bone (Femur)) | site : Upper &lower limbs
structure: 2 ends (epiphysis) & a shaft (diaphysis).
*Epiphysis;
• Expanded upper & lower ends of long bone.
• It has smooth articular surface covered by articular hyaline cartilage.
*Diaphysis;
• Compact bone tube, with central medullary cavity filled with bone marrow (soft vascular tissue).
• Separated from epiphysis by epiphyseal plate of hyaline cartilage, responsible for bone growth in length.
• Surrounded by periosteum (fibrous sheath), responsible for bone growth in width.
N.B. Metaphysis; Upper & lower parts of diaphysis just below epiphyseal cartilage (most active part of long bone).
SHORT BONES (Short Bone (Carpal)) | site : Carpal bones in hands & Tarsal bones in foot
structure:
• Spongy (cancellous) bone covered by compact bone.
FLAT BONES (Flat Bone (Frontal)) | site : Scapula, ribs & skull cap (roof) bones.
structure:
• 2 plates of compact bone with middle layer of spongy bone.
N.B.: In skull bones 2 layers of compact are called outer & inner tables while spongy layer is called diploe.
Function: Protection & muscle attachment.
IRREGULAR BONES (Irregular Bone (vertebra)) | site : Bones with projecting processes as vertebrae.
structure:
• Spongy (cancellous) bone covered by compact bone.
PNEUMATIC BONES | site : Skull bones around nose (frontal & maxillary), containing air cavities (paranasal air sinuses).
structure:
• Contains one air cavity (maxillary sinus) or multiple small cells (mastoid air cells).
Function: Decrease skull weight, resonance of voice & warming of inspired air by vascular mucosa..
SESAMOID BONES | site : Patella; largest sesamoid bone, embedded in quadriceps femoris tendon infront knee.
structure: Small bone nodules embedded in some muscle tendons.
Function: Diminish friction between tendons & bones.

sections.heading: GROWTH OF LONG BONES
sections.text:
| Growth in width (Periosteum) | Growth in length (Epiphyseal plate of cartilage)
DEF: | Fibrous sheath around shaft of long bone. | Plate of cartilage between epiphysis & diaphysis of long bone.
STRUCTURE: | -Outer layer: White fibrous tissue.
-Inner layer: Contains osteoblasts for bone growth in width | Hyaline cartilage.
FUNCTION: | — | Bone growth in length by proliferation of its cells. When bone becomes mature, it stops division & ossifies resulting in fusion between epiphysis & diaphysis under hormonal control & 2 years earlier in females. It ossifies at one end 2-3 years earlier than the other end which is called the growing end.

sections.heading: ARTERIAL SUPPLY OF LONG BONES
sections.text:
Artery | Book text
Nutrient artery | • Enters shaft at its middle through oblique nutrient foramen & runs away from growing end.
• Supplies inner 2/3 of shaft & bone marrow.
Metaphyseal arteries | Enter through minute foramina to supply metaphysis.
Epiphyseal arteries | • Supply epiphysis.
• Anastomose with metaphyseal arteries after ossification of epiphyseal cartilage.
Periosteal arteries | Supply outer 1/3 shaft & anastomose with other arteries.

sections.heading: B) Cartilage — PROPERTIES:
sections.text:
*Rubbery type of connective tissue (tough & resilient), resisting friction & compression forces.
*It consists of mature cartilage cells (chondrocytes), fibers and matrix. It has no blood vessels (nutrition is by diffusion from blood vessels of perichondrium), nerves or lymphatics.
*Great growth capacity by multiplication of chondroblasts (immature cartilage cells).

sections.heading: B) Cartilage — TYPES:
sections.text:
Type | Book text
HYALINE (GLASS LIKE) (most widespread in human body) | Cartilage: Numerous small rounded cells.
Matrix: Translucent.
Sites:
• Developing bones in fetus.
• Epiphyseal plates of long bones.
• Articular cartilage in joints.
• Cartilages of larynx (except epiglottis) & tracheal rings.
• Xiphoid process (sternum) & costal cartilages.
Ossification: In certain sites; epiphyseal cartillages& Larynx
PNEUMATIC BONES [heading exactly as printed on p.18; the book's figure on p.19 labels this block “White fibrocartilage”] | Cartilage: Few.
Matrix: Opaque, rich in collagen bundles.
Sites:
• Intervertebral discs.
Ossification: Does not occur
YELLOW ELASTIC FIBROCARTILAGE | Cartilage: Abundant.
Matrix: Yellow, rich in yellow elastic fibers.
Sites:
• Tip of nose.
• Auricle of ear.
• Epiglottis of larynx
Ossification: Does not occur

sections.heading: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Contact of 2 or more bones

sections.heading: CLASSIFICATION: 1-FIBROUS JOINTS — Bones are connected by fibrous tissue, fixed (immobile) joint
sections.text:
Sutures | Gomphosis | Syndesmosis
-In skull.
-Bones are connected by fibrous tissue (sutural ligament).
-Obliterated in old age. | -In teeth.
-Roots of teeth are connected to sockets in mandible & maxilla by fibrous tissue (periodontal ligament). | -In inf. tibio-fibular joint.
-Lower ends of tibia & fibula are connected by fibrous tissue (interosseous ligament).

sections.heading: 2-CARTILAGENOUS JOINTS — Bones are connected by cartilaginous tissue
sections.text:
| Primary | Secondary
Example : | Epiphyseal plate | Intervertebral discs.
Site: | At ends of growing long bones between epiphysis & diaphysis. | Midline.
Type: | Hyaline. | White fibrocartilage disc (articulating surfaces are covered by thin hyaline cartilage). It is strengthened by ligaments which do not fuse to form complete capsule.
Ossification: | Temporary, disappears by ossification. | Permanent.
Mobility: | Immobile. | Limited mobility (facilitated by white fibrocartilage elasticity).

sections.heading: 3-SYNOVIAL JOINTS — Freely mobile, present mostly in limbs
sections.text:
Component | Book text
Fibrous capsule | *Joint is surrounded by strong fibrous capsule, which is lined by synovial membrane & supported by strong ligaments.
Articular cartilage | *Articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage, which is smooth & lubricated by synovial fluid. *It has no blood vessels or nerves (nutrition is from synovial fluid). *In old age it shows irregularities due to erosion (eroded areas do not repair).
Joint cavity | Potential cavity, containing thin film of synovial fluid. It becomes manifest if fluid, blood or pus collect in it.
Synovial membrane | *Thin, moist & glistening, covers all structures inside joint except articular surfaces & lines capsule. *It secretes & absorbs synovial fluid.
Synovial fluid | Pale yellow viscus similar to egg albumin (containing synovial cells, macrophages & lymphocytes).
*It lubricates, helps in nutrition & reduces erosion of articular cartilage.
Ligaments | Capsular, extra & intra capsular ligaments, support & strengthen the joint.
Structures inside cavity of some synovial joints | -Articular fibro-cartilagenous disc: Temporo-mandibular joint (divides joint cavity into upper & lower compartments).
-Menisci: Knee joint (semilunar plates of fibro-cartilage).
-Ligaments: Cruciate ligaments in knee joint.
-Tendon: Tendon long head biceps in shoulder joint.

sections.heading: FACTORS AFFECTING STABILITY OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS:
sections.text:
1-Shape & fitting of articulating surfaces
2-Thickness & elasticity of capsule.
3-Position & strength of ligaments
4-Strength of surrounding muscles.

sections.heading: FACTORS AFFECTING RANGE OF MOVEMENTS OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS:
sections.text:
1-Tension of surrounding ligaments
2-Contraction of antagonistic muscles.
3-Approximation & contact of soft tissues around joint.

sections.heading: NERVE SUPPLY OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS:
sections.text:
Hiltons law: N. supply to a muscle acting on specific joint, gives branch to joint & another branch to skin covering joint.
N.B.: Nerves supplying joint (articular nerves) end in fibrous capsule & related ligaments. They are sensitive to pain, position & movement of joint.

sections.heading: MOVEMENTS
sections.text:
Movement | Meaning | Movement | Meaning
-Flexion: | Bending (approximation of 2 ventral aspects). | -Extension: | Straightening (2 ventral aspects move away from each other).
-Abduction: | Movement of limb away from midline (middle finger in hand,second toe in foot). | -Adduction: | Movement of limb towards midline (middle finger in hand, second toe in foot).
-Circumduction: | Combination of all above movements. | -Rotation: | Medially or laterally around a vertical axis.
-Supination: | Lateral rotation forearm | -Pronation: | Medial rotation forearm.
-Inversion: | Sole directed inwards. | -Eversion: | Sole directed outwards.
-Opposition: | Thumb comes in contact with other 4 fingers. | -Gliding: | Non axial movement.

sections.heading: CLINICAL IMPORTANCE:
sections.text:
1.Cavity is swollen due to fluid, pus or blood collection.
2.Articular surfaces are eroded & rough in osteoarthritis or overweight (painful).
3.Separation of articular surfaces is called dislocation.

sections.heading: TYPES (VARIETIES) OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS — A- According to the number of articulating bones:
sections.text:
1. Simple joints: Between 2 bones ; shoulder.
2. Compound joints: Between more than two bones ; elbow.
3. Complex joints: Contain intra-articular structures ; knee.

sections.heading: B- According to axis of movement & shape of the articular surfaces: I. UNI-AXIAL JOINTS (SINGLE AXIS)
sections.text:
Joint | Book text
A- Hinge joint | The convex articular surface is trochlea-like; elbow joint. The movement is only flexion and extension around a transverse axis due to strong collateral ligaments.
B- Pivot joint | Articulating surfaces consist of a central bony axis surrounded by a fibro-osseous ring; superior radio-ulnar joint. The movement is rotation around a longitudinal axis .

sections.heading: II. BI-AXIAL JOINTS (2 AXIS)
sections.text:
Joint | Book text
A-Condylar joint | 2 separate convex surfaces (condyles) which articulate with 2 concave surfaces, ; knee joint (bicondylar) or 1 condyle articulating with 1 concave surface ; temporomandibular joint (unicondylar).
B- Ellipsoid joint | Oval convex surface (carpal bones) with elliptical concave surface (inferior surface of radius & articular disc of ulna) ; wrist joint.
C- Saddle joint | Surfaces are concavo-convex ; carpometacarpal joint of thumb.

sections.heading: III. MULTI-AXIAL JOINTS (3 AXIS) — Ball & socket
sections.text: Globular rounded bone articulates with concave socket (most freely mobile); shoulder & hip joints.

sections.heading: IV. NON-AXIAL JOINTS — Plane
sections.text: Articular surfaces are flat & movement is gliding ; inter-carpal joints, superior tibio-fibular joint & intervertebral joints.

sections.text: Muscle tissue has property of contraction, which is capacity of muscle fibers to become short.

sections.heading: Q. SKELETAL MUSCLES ATTACHMENT:
sections.text:
• Each muscle has 2 attachments:
*Origin; most fixed attachment
*Insertion; most mobile attachment.
• In limbs, origin is usually proximal to insertion & during contraction; insertion moves towards origin. Sometimes insertion is fixed while origin is mobile. A muscle may have more than one point of origin or insertion.

sections.heading: Q. TYPES OF SKELETAL MUSCLES ATTACHMENT:
sections.text:
• Attachment to bone; commonest, by flesh or by tendon.
• Attachment to skin; muscles of face.
• Attachment to fibrous raphe; mylohyoid muscles.
• Attachment to cartilage; muscles of larynx.

sections.heading: Q. ACTION OF SKELETAL MUSCLES:
sections.text:
1-Prime mover(agonist) : It initiates & maintains a movement .
2-Antagonist: It opposes action of prime mover.
3-Fixator (stabilizer): It fixes origin of prime mover or stabilize joint acted upon.
4-Synergist: Sometimes prime mover muscle crosses many joints before reaching insertion. Synergistic muscles contract to eliminate unwanted movement at crossed joints, so action of prime mover at desired joint become maximal.

sections.heading: A) CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM — Brain
sections.text:
site : Inside skull.
Parts:
• Cerebrum (2 cerebral hemispheres): 4 lobes; (frontal, parietal, occipital & temporal).
• Cerebellum.
• Brainstem; Midbrain, pons & medulla oblongata.
• Diencephalon; Thalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus, metathalamus & epi thalamus

sections.heading: A) CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM — Meninges
sections.text: Coverings of C.N.S, arranged as pia, arachnoid & dura mater (((from inside to outside))).

sections.heading: A) CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM — Spinal cord
sections.text:
site : Inside vertebral column, 45 cm long & its end is tapering (conus medullaris).
Segments : 31 (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral & 1 coccygeal).
End : Tapering (conus medullaris).
2 enlargements: Cervical & lumbar, where N. plexuses arise.
Structure:
*Outer white matter; nerve fibers forming tracts.
*Inner gray matter; nerve cells. H-shaped;
• 2 ventral horns (motor nuclei).
• 2 dorsal horns (sensory nuclei).
• 2 lat. horns (contain sympathetic nuclei in thoracic & upper 2 lumbar segments while contain para-sympathetic nuclei in 2nd, 3rd & 4th sacral segments).
*Central canal.

sections.heading: B) PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM — Nerves: Spinal
sections.text:
-From spinal cord.
-31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral & 1 coccygeal.
-Arises by 2 roots;
*Ant. (ventral): Contains motor fibers
*Post. (dorsal): Contains sensory fibers.
-Both roots unite forming mixed trunk which divides into mixed ant. & post. rami.

sections.text:

sections.heading: 1 Heart — SITE:
sections.text: Behind sternum & costal cartilages (from 2nd to 6th) , ⅔ Of Heart lies to Lt. & 1/3 of heart lies to Rt. of median plane

sections.heading: 1 Heart — CHAMBERS: Four (2 atria & 2 ventricles);
sections.text:
Chamber | Book text
Rt. atrium | Receives deoxygenated blood from all body through 2 large veins (S.V.C & I.V.C), sends it to Rt. ventricle through tricuspid valve.
Lt. atrium | Receives oxygenated blood from lungs through 4 pulmonary veins, sends it to Lt. ventricle through mitral valve.
Rt. ventricle | Pumps deoxygenated blood through pulmonary valve to pulmonary trunk which divides into 2 branches (one for each lung) to be oxygenated.
Lt. ventricle | Pumps oxygenated blood to all parts of body through aortic valve to aorta & its branches.

sections.heading: 1 Heart — N.B.:
sections.text:
* Rt. 1/2 contains deoxygenated (venous) blood, while Lt. 1/2 contains oxygenated (arterial) blood.
* Heart is covered by 2 pericardial sacs; fibrous & serous pericardium

sections.heading: BLOOD CIRCULATION: 3 TYPES
sections.text:
Circulation | Book text
SYSTEMIC | - Begins in Lt. ventricle, where oxygenated blood passes through aortic valve to aorta & its branches to all body tissues for exchange of gases & materials.
-Deoxygenated blood is collected by small then large veins & finally by S.V.C & I.V.C into Rt. atrium, which sends it through tricuspid valve to Rt. ventricle where this circulation ends.
PULMONARY | -Begins in Rt. ventricle, where deoxygenated blood passes through pulmonary valve to pulmonary artery & its 2 branches to both lungs for exchange of gases.
-Oxygenated blood returns through 4 pulmonary veins to Lt. atrium, which sends it through mitral valve to Lt. ventricle where this circulation ends & a new cycle starts.
PORTAL | -Venous blood collected from stomach, intestine, pancreas & spleen is collected by portal vein, which enters porta hepatis of liver & divides into branches ending in liver sinusoids.
-Blood leaves sinusoids by hepatic veins ending in I.V.C.
-It transmits venous blood from GIT to liver, to metabolize undigested nutrients & to detoxify blood.

sections.heading: 2 blood vessels — ARTERIES — DEFINITION:
sections.text: Blood vessel carrying oxygenated blood from heart to periphery, except pulmonary & umbilical arteries which carry deoxygenated blood.

sections.heading: ARTERIES — CLASSIFICATION:
sections.text: According to size & structure into; large sized, medium sized & small arteries.

sections.heading: ARTERIAL ANASTMOSIS — DEF / FUNCTION
sections.text:
DEF: communication between arteries, mainly around joints.
FUNCTION:
• Increase blood supply to some organs as stomach.
• Equalize pressure in communicating arteries.
• Maintains blood flow to body area or part if main artery is obstructed

sections.heading: ARTERIAL ANASTMOSIS — TYPES:
sections.text:
Type | Def. | Example
By end to end | 2 ends of 2 arteries are connected forming arch. | In hand & foot, between gastric arteries, between gut arteries, between ant. & post. intercostal AA.
By Terminal arterioles | *Lie around joints, between branches of main A. above joint & its branches below joint. *In gradual obstruction of main A., it will open to maintain blood supply below obstruction. | Anastomosis around elbow.
By convergence | 2 arteries converge uniting together. | Anastomosis between the 2 vertebral AA.

sections.heading: ARTERIES — CLINICAL IMPORTANCE:
sections.text:
• Large AA. crossing over a joint are liable to be kinked during joint movement. Distal blood flow is not interrupted because there is adequate anastomosis between branches proximal & distal to joint.
• Sudden closure of main A. by faulty ligation, will lead to death of limb part distal to closure because anastomosis is does not open in sudden closure.

sections.heading: *End arteries: Arteries which do not anastomose with adjacent arteries & their obstruction lead to death (necrosis) of tissues supplied
sections.text:
1-Central retinal A.: Supplies retina
2-Pulmonary AA.
3-Central branches of cerebral AA.
4-Renal A.: Supplies kidney
5-Splenic A.: Supplies spleen.

sections.heading: VEINS — DEF:
sections.text: Blood vessel carrying deoxygenated blood from periphery to heart, except pulmonary & umbilical veins which carry oxygenated blood.

sections.heading: FACTORS HELPING VENOUS RETURN:
sections.text:
1-From upper part body: Gravity.
2-From lower part body:
A)lower limb:
• Venous valves
• Arterial pulsations.
• Muscle contraction (pump)
• Deep fascia around muscle groups.
• Negative intra-thoracic pressure draws blood from abdomen, head & neck into thorax.
B)Abdomen, pelvis & thorax:
• Venous return by suction mechanism of -ve intrathoracic pressure.

sections.heading: ARTERIO-VENOUS CONNECTIONS — Arteries & veins are connected by:
sections.text:
1-Capillaries; narrow uniform diameter.
2-Sinusoids; wide irregular diameter with dilatations & constrictions.
3-Arterio-venous shunt; between small AA. & accompanying VV.

sections.heading: ARTERIO-VENOUS SHUNT — SITES:
sections.text:
*External ear, nail bed & palmar aspects of digits.
*Tongue *Thyroid gland *Penis *Alimentary tract.

sections.heading: ARTERIO-VENOUS SHUNT — CHARACTERS:
sections.text: Straight or coiled, surrounded by thick muscular coat & supplied by sympathetic fibers controlling its opening & closure.

sections.heading: ARTERIO-VENOUS SHUNT — FUNCTIONS:
sections.text:
1-Regulation of body temperature & local heat; on opening blood pass from A. to V. decreasing local heat.
2-Regulation of food absorption
3-Play role in erection.

sections.heading: CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: *Varicose veins & stagnation*
sections.text:
A varicosed vein is one with larger diameter than normal, elongated & tortuous. It may be due to hereditary weakness of veins walls, incompetent valves & elevated intra-abdominal pressure (due to multiple pregnancies or abdominal tumors).
Blood escapes from deep to superficial VV. leading to varicosity which is common in lower limbs. Blood stagnation in varicose veins leads to thrombosis (as deep venous thrombosis in calf muscles).

sections.heading: LYMPHATIC SYSTEM — Definition
sections.text: -System responsible for lymph (clear colorless fluid rich in proteins) circulation from tissue spaces (intercellular spaces) to blood stream.

sections.heading: IT CONSISTS OF:
sections.text:
1. Lymph vessels.
2. Lymphoid tissue (lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils & thymus)
3. B & T Lymphocytes (free cells).

sections.heading: LYMPH VESSELS
sections.text:
-Fine vessels in tissue spaces, unite together forming larger lymph vessels which join lymph nodes.
1-Afferent vessels: Carry lymph to lymph nodes (open in periphery at convex border).
2-Efferent vessels: Carry lymph away from lymph nodes (emerge from hilum).

sections.heading: LYMPH VESSELS — CHARACTERS:
sections.text:
*End blindly in tissue spaces, containing wide pores for fat & protein passage.
*Have many valves allowing lymph flow in one direction.
*Absent in brain, spinal cord, bone marrow & avascular structures (cartilage, cornea & hair).
-All lymph vessels are collected in 2 large lymph ducts in root of neck;
*Thoracic duct: Drains Lt. side head & neck, Lt. upper limb, Lt. side thorax & body below diaphragm.
*Rt. lymphatic duct: Drains Rt. side head & neck, Rt. upper limb & Rt. side thorax.
-Both ducts open in 2 large veins at root of neck.

sections.heading: FACTORS HELPING LYMPH FLOW & MOVEMENT:
sections.text:
* Arterial pulsation * Muscular contraction
* Negative intra-thoracic pressure * Peristaltic intestinal movement

sections.heading: LYMPH NODES — DEF / SITE
sections.text:
DEF: oval or kidney small bodies.
SITE: Along lymph vessels course, in groups at fixed sites;
• In neck; on sides & at junction with head.
• In chest; Close to trachea & bronchi & in chest wall.
• In abdomen; around abdominal aorta & close to abdominal organs.
• In pelvis; around blood vessels & close to pelvic organs.
• In root of upper limb; axillary lymph nodes.
• In root of lower limb; inguinal lymph nodes.

sections.heading: LYMPH NODES — FUNCTIONS:
sections.text:
• Filtration of lymph from bacteria & foreign bodies.
• Formation & production of lymphocytes.
• Site of interaction between micro-organisms (antigens) & lymphocytes & phagocytes .

sections.heading: SPLEEN — SITE / SIZE
sections.text:
SITE: Haemo-lymphatic organ, in upper left part of abdominal cavity below left dome of diaphragm, behind stomach & protected by 9th, 10th & 11th ribs
SIZE: Not palpable, unless enlarged at least 3 times.

sections.heading: SPLEEN — FUNCTIONS:
sections.text:
• In fetus plays role in blood cell formation.
• In adult it stores & concentrates blood cells to be used in hemorrhage.Size
• Destroys old expired red cells.
• Filters blood from any harmful substances (spleen filters blood while lymph nodes filter lymph).

sections.heading: Thymus gland:
sections.text: Lymphatic organ with endocrine function (secretes thymosine hormone). It is formed of 2 lobes & lies behind sternum (its size increases until puberty then it decreases with age advance).

sections.heading: LYMPHATIC — CLINICAL IMPORTANCE:
sections.text:
- Extensive destruction of lymph vessels (in surgery) or obstruction (in filariasis) leads to edema of part drained.
- Lymph nodes may swell in inflammation, metastases or by primary tumor (lymph drainage of all body organs including skin should be known).
- In lymph node enlargement, area drained should be examined & in any lesion draining lymph nodes should be examined.

sections.heading:
A COVALENT BONDS
03 CHEMICAL BONDS
sections.text:
•Covalent bond is formed by sharing of a pair of electrons or more between adjacent atoms.
•They are strong bonds; considerable energy must be expended to break covalent bonds.

•According to the polarity of covalent bonds, they are classified into:

sections.heading:
1 Nonpolar Covalent Bond
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › A COVALENT BONDS
sections.text:
•Bond between 2 atoms that have the same electronegativity (Power to attract electrons)
•Therefore have equal sharing of electrons.

sections.heading:
2 Polar Covalent Bond
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › A COVALENT BONDS
sections.text:
•Bond between 2 atoms that have different electronegativity
•Therefore have unequal sharing of electrons.
•The shared electronsare attracted to the more electronegative atom.
•Such covalent bond ispolar & will have a dipole (One end is positive δ+& the other end isnegative δ-) as in water molecules.

sections.heading:
B NONCOVALENT BONDS OR FORCES
03 CHEMICAL BONDS
sections.text:
•These are weaker than covalent bonds.
•They play an important role in determining many of properties of biomolecules & how these molecules interact with water and with each other.
•They include:

sections.heading:
1 Hydrogen Bonds
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › B NONCOVALENT BONDS OR FORCES
sections.text:
•They are weak noncovalent interaction between the hydrogen (δ+) of one molecule & the more electronegative atom (δ-) of an acceptor molecule.

•Examples of hydrogen bonding are:
▪Hydrogen bonds between water molecules or between water & other molecules.
▪Hydrogen bonds responsible for
▸Protein folding into three-dimensional forms (Explained later with protein structure)
▸DNA stability (Explained later with DNA structure).

sections.heading:
2 Electrostatic Interactions (Salt Bridge or Ionic Bonds)
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › B NONCOVALENT BONDS OR FORCES
sections.text:
•Ions are electrically charged particles formed when atoms lose or gain electrons.
•Electrostatic interactions or ionic bonds occur between:
▪Oppositely charged ions (Na+& Cl-)
▪Oppositely charged groups (NH3+& COO-).

sections.heading:
3 Van der Waals Forces
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › B NONCOVALENT BONDS OR FORCES
sections.text:
•They are transient attraction between molecules at a distance → Van der Waals distance.
•Van der Waal force is due to constant motion of electrons that will cause, atany instant, asymmetric distribution of electrons.
•The attraction between molecules is greatest at the Van der Waals distance.
•If molecules approach each other more closely, a repulsive force develops, by the negative charges of their outer electron shells.

sections.heading:
4 Hydrophobic Interactions
03 CHEMICAL BONDS › B NONCOVALENT BONDS OR FORCES
sections.text: •Hydrophobic interaction refers to the tendency of non polar compounds to cluster together in an aqueous medium, as in case of oil and water.

sections.heading: 01 BIOLOGICAL IMPORTANCE AND FUNCTIONS OF PROTEINS:
sections.text:
•Provide the body with essential amino acids, nitrogen, and sulfur.
•Enzymes are mainly protein in nature.
•Many hormones are peptides or protein in nature (e.g., glucagon and insulin).
•The antibodies (Immunoglobulins) which play an important role in the body's defensive mechanisms are protein in nature.
•Hemoglobin is a chromoprotein. It carries O2from the lungs to tissues.
•Plasma proteins are responsible for the most effective osmotic pressure of blood. This osmotic pressure plays a central role in many processes e.g., water distribution & urine formation.
•Plasma proteins help the transport of many substances in the blood e.g., lipids, hormones (e.g., thyroid hormones) and minerals (e.g., calcium, iron, and copper).
•Very important components of different types of cell membranes as receptors & transporters.

sections.heading: 02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•Different Levels of Protein Structure :
▪Proteins in their native state are characterized by their three-dimensional structure.
▪Proteins formed of one polypeptide chain have primary, secondary and tertiary structures.
▪Proteins formed of two or more polypeptide chains have an additional quaternary structure.
Structure of proteins can be divided into four orders:

sections.heading:
A PRIMARY STRUCTURE:
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•The primary structure refers to the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide chain.
•The primary structure is stabilized by peptide bonds, which are made during the process of protein biosynthesis.
•The amino acid sequence of any protein is specific to that protein.
•The polypeptide chain starts on the left side by amino acid number 1, which contains a free terminal amino group and termed N-terminus amino acid.
•On the right side, at the end, the polypeptide chain contains an amino acid with a free terminal carboxylic group and termed C-terminus amino acid.
•The synthesis of the polypeptide chain starts from the N-terminus end toward the C-terminus.
•The amino acids sequence is determined by the genetic information present in the DNA.

sections.heading:
B SECONDARY STRUCTURE
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS
sections.text: Includes 2 main regular forms:

sections.heading:
1 Helix
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › B SECONDARY STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•It is the folding of the polypeptide chain along its longitudinal axis, into a specific coiled structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds.
•Each hydrogen bond is formed between the NH group of an amino acid & the C=O group of an amino acid located exactly four residues earlier in the sequence.
•The R-groups of amino acids project outwards of the helix.
•Folding can be right- or left-handed:
▪Right-handed in most proteins
▪Left-handed in collagen

sections.heading:
2 β -Pleated Sheet
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › B SECONDARY STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•If two or more segments of the single polypeptide chain are arranged side by side, β-pleated sheet will be formed and is stabilized by hydrogen bonds.
•The R-groups of amino acids project above or below the plane of the sheet.

sections.heading:
N.B
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › B SECONDARY STRUCTURE › 2 β -Pleated Sheet
sections.text: •An individual protein may contain both types of secondary structure.

sections.heading:
C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•It is folding of polypeptide chain of a protein into a specific three-dimensional globular structure.
•This structure is stabilized by different types of of bonds or interactions as follows:

sections.heading:
1 Hydrophobic interactions
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
sections.text:
•Refer to the tendency of nonpolar compounds to cluster together in an aqueous medium.
•The nonpolar side chains of neutral amino acids tend to associate together in proteins.

sections.heading:
2 Electrostatic bonds (salt bridges or ionic bonds)
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
sections.text:
•They are formed between oppositely charged groups of amino acid side chains.
•Example: Lysine (positively charged) and aspartic acid (negatively charged) at physiological or body pH.

sections.heading:
3 Disulfide Bonds
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
sections.text: •They are present in many proteins, when two cysteine are connected to form cystine e.g., keratin and insulin.

sections.heading:
4 Hydrogen bonds
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
sections.text:
•Amino acid side chains are involved in hydrogen bonds formation:
▪The hydroxyl groups of some amino acids (e.g., serine, threonine),
▪The amide groups of glutamine and asparagine
▪The carboxyl groups of aspartic and glutamic acids
▪The ring nitrogen of histidine participate in formation of internal hydrogen bonds.

sections.heading:
5 Van der Waals interactions
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS › C TERTIARY STRUCTURE:
sections.text:
•They are transient attractions between molecules at a distance called the Van der Waals distance.
•These weak interactions also contribute to the stability of proteins.

sections.heading:
D QUATERNARY STRUCTURE
02 STRUCTURE OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•This order is shown only by certain types of proteins which have two or more polypeptide chains (Several subunits or polymers).
•Each subunit has its own primary, secondary & tertiary structure and the subunits combine forming the quaternary structure.
•High level of organization may be essential for activity of certain proteins (Enzymes & hemoglobin).
•Forces that stabilize subunits of this structure are similar to those stabilizing tertiary structure.

sections.heading: 03 PROTEIN FOLDING AND CHAPERONES

Protein folding
03 PROTEIN FOLDING AND CHAPERONES
sections.text:
•The process by which a protein, after being synthesized by a ribosome as a linear chain of amino acids, changes from an unstable random coil into a more ordered & functionally active 3D structure.
•The folding process is helped by a complex network of molecular proteins called “Chaperones”
•They use different mechanisms to promote efficient protein folding & prevent their aggregation.
•An age-related decline in chaperones activity contributes to the development of various protein-aggregation diseases, including Alzheimer's disease & Parkinson's disease.

sections.heading: 04 DENATURATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•Denaturation is a specific property of proteins.
•It involves the change of the natural state "Native state" of proteins.
•It is due to the rupture of chemical bonds that stabilize the secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structures leaving the protein in its primary structure.
•It may be reversible or irreversible and may result in protein coagulation as albumin coagulation by heat (Due to formation of disulfide cross linkage).

sections.heading:
1 Physical agents
04 DENATURATION OF PROTEINS › A FACTORS THAT PRODUCE DENATURATION
sections.text: •As heat, mechanical agitation, sonication, ultraviolet irradiation, X-ray etc....

sections.heading:
2 Chemical agents
04 DENATURATION OF PROTEINS › A FACTORS THAT PRODUCE DENATURATION
sections.text: •As acids, alkalis, alcohols, urea, salts of heavy metals like Pb+2, Ag+2, Cu+2etc....

sections.heading:
B EFFECTS OF DENATURATION ON PROTEINS
04 DENATURATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
•Loss of the secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure of proteins.
•Increased viscosity.
•Decreased solubility due to exposure of nonpolar hydrophobic groups.
•Increased digestibility by proteolytic enzymes due to exposure of peptide bonds.
•Loss of biologic activity e.g., inactivation of enzymes.
•Loss of antigenic property as injection of denatured protein cannot induce antibody formation within the body, in contrast to the action of native proteins.

sections.heading: 05 CONFORMATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: Depending on their conformation, proteins are classified into 2 major classes

sections.heading:
A FIBROUS PROTEINS
05 CONFORMATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: •They consist of polypeptide chains that are arranged in a parallel form along a single axis to yield long fibers or sheets. e.g., collagen, elastin, and α-keratin.

sections.heading:
B GLOBULAR PROTEINS:
05 CONFORMATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: •They are tightly folded into compact spherical or globular shapes. e.g., most enzymes, hemoglobin, myoglobin, many hormones, immunoglobulins, and plasma proteins.

sections.heading: 06 CHEMICAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text:
Depending on their chemical composition & structural complexity,
Proteins are classified into three main groups:

sections.heading:
A SIMPLE PROTEINS:
06 CHEMICAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: •On hydrolysis, they produce amino acids only, e.g. albumins.

sections.heading:
B CONJUGATED PROTEINS:
06 CHEMICAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: •On hydrolysis, they produce amino acids & other groups (Prosthetic groups) as hemoproteins are formed of protein part attached to heme.

sections.heading:
C DERIVED PROTEINS:
06 CHEMICAL CLASSIFICATION OF PROTEINS
sections.text: •These are derived from the above mentioned groups by hydrolysis or denaturation.

sections.heading:
A DEFINITION
01 INTRODUCTION TO ENZYMES
sections.text: •Enzymes are biocatalysts that regulate the rate of biochemical reactions.

sections.heading:
B COMMON FEATURES
01 INTRODUCTION TO ENZYMES
sections.text:
•All are produced by living cells and can act outside these cells.
•They are needed in very small amounts.
•They accelerate the reaction without affecting its equilibrium point.
•They are mainly protein in nature, but some RNAs have catalytic activity (e.g., ribozymes).
•They are not changed chemically by the end of the reaction.
•They are highly specific (act on a specific substrate or inter-related substrates).

sections.heading:
C NOMENCLATURE
01 INTRODUCTION TO ENZYMES
sections.text:
•Most enzyme names have the suffix “-ase” attached to the substrate of the reaction (e.g. glucosidase, urease, sucrase).
•Some describe the action performed (Lactate dehydrogenase & adenylyl cyclase).
•Other enzymes retain their original names (As trypsin & pepsin).

sections.heading:
D ENZYME SPECIFICITY
01 INTRODUCTION TO ENZYMES
sections.text:
•Enzymes are highly specific in their action.
•They interact with :
▪One substrate (e.g., lactase acts on lactose only) or few specific substrates
▪Catalyze only 1 type of chemical reaction (e.g: hexokinase enzyme acts on hexoses).
•Specificity of enzymes is due to the nature & arrangement of chemical groups at the active site.
•This allows the enzyme to bind and activate only one substrate or a small number of structurally related substrates.

sections.heading:
E CHEMICAL NATURE
01 INTRODUCTION TO ENZYMES
sections.text:
•Enzymes are either simple or conjugated proteins (Holoenzymes)
•Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme (Protein part) + Cofactor (Non-protein part).
•Cofactors are molecules required for activity of holoenzymes & they are:
▪Organic (e.g. NAD and FAD)
▪Inorganic (e.g. metals)

sections.heading: 02 MECHANISM OF ENZYME ACTION
sections.text:
•The catalytic action of an enzyme is explained by:
▪Binding of the substrate to the active site of the enzyme.
▪Lowering of the activation energy required for the reaction.

sections.heading:
A BINDING OF THE SUBSTRATE TO THE ACTIVE SITE OF THE ENZYME
02 MECHANISM OF ENZYME ACTION
sections.text:
•The enzyme molecule contains a special pocket called the “Active site”.
•The amino acids at the active site are arranged in a very precise manner that creates a 3D surface complementary to the substrate.
•The induced fit model states that when a specific substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme forming an enzyme–substrate (ES) complex.
•It induces conformational changes of enzyme

allowing more fitting & catalysis (Induction).

sections.heading:
B LOWERING OF THE ACTIVATION ENERGY
02 MECHANISM OF ENZYME ACTION
sections.text:
•For the reactants to be converted into products, a minimum amount of energy called “Activation energy” is required.
•Enzyme accelerates the reaction by lowering the energy of activation without affecting the equilibrium of the reaction.
•∆G is the change in the free energy of the reaction:
∆G = Energy of the products B – Energy of the reactants A
•The enzyme does not affect the free energy change of the reaction (∆G)
•Therefore, does not change the equilibrium of the reaction.

sections.heading: 03 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE (VELOCITY)
sections.text:
•When studying effect of any factor on enzyme catalysis, only one factor should be varied at a time, while all other factors are kept constant.
•The rate of the reaction should always be measured at the very beginning of the reaction
•The so-called initial velocity (V0or Vi), to avoid by time decrease of substrate concentration, accumulation of products and equilibrium.

sections.heading:
A EFFECT OF SUBSTRATE CONCENTRATION [S]
03 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE (VELOCITY)
sections.text:
•The velocity of the reaction increases as the substrate concentration [S] increases up to a point where the enzyme is said to be saturated.
•At this point enzyme concentration is the limiting factor.
•The measured initial velocity or VIincreases to a maximum value Vmax.
•The substrate concentration that produces half the maximal velocity is termed Michaelis constant or Km.

•Smaller KMreflects higher affinity of the enzyme to its substrate (Km1 < Km2 in diagram) and vice versa.

sections.heading:
B EFFECT OF ENZYME CONCENTRATION (E)
03 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE (VELOCITY)
sections.text:
•The velocity of the reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of the enzyme.
•This is true up to a point when a further increase in the enzyme concentration is not accompanied by an increase in the velocity of the reaction.
•At this point the substrate is said to be the limiting factor.

sections.heading:
C EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE
03 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE (VELOCITY)
sections.text:
•At 0°C enzyme action virtually stops due to the inhibition of movement and collision between the substrate and enzyme molecules.
•As the temperature rises:
▪Velocity of the reaction increases due to increased kinetic energy of molecules & increased collision between substrate & enzyme molecules, increasing the formation of ES complex.
▪The increase in velocity of reaction continues up to a point “The optimum temperature”, beyond which any further increase in temperature causes a decrease in reaction rate.
•The optimum temperature for most animal enzymes is about 37°C.
•The optimum temperature for most plant enzymes is about 50°C.
•For most enzymes, the activity virtually stops at around 70°C., due to denaturation of the enzyme protein, disrupting the organization of the active site.

sections.heading:
D EFFECT OF PH
03 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE (VELOCITY)
sections.text:
•Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it shows maximal activity.
•Activity decreases as we go away from the optimum pH.
•It virtually stops at about 2 units of pH above or below this pH.
•Slight changes in pH cause marked changes in enzyme activity due to alteration of the charges on the substrate and the active site of the enzyme.
•Extreme changes of pH cause denaturation and irreversible inhibition of enzyme action.
•Most enzymes have an optimum pH between 5 and 9.
•There are some exceptions, for example:
▪Pepsin, a digestive enzyme in the stomach, is maximally active at pH 2
▪Whereas other enzymes, designed to work at neutral pH, are denatured by such an acidic environment.

sections.heading:
A SHORT-TERM REGULATION
04 REGULATION OF ENZYME ACTIVITY
sections.text:
•It occurs within seconds by changing activity of the enzyme & is achieved through:
▪Availability of cofactors or substrates
▪Presence of enzyme inhibitors or activators
▪Covalent modification: Reversible phosphorylation/ dephosphorylation

sections.heading:
B LONG-TERM REGULATION
04 REGULATION OF ENZYME ACTIVITY
sections.text:
•It takes hours or days to change amount of the enzyme & is achieved through:
▪Increasing (or decreasing) degradation of the enzyme.
▪Increasing synthesis (Induction) or decreasing synthesis (Repression) of the enzyme by regulation of gene expression.

sections.heading: 05 ENZYME INHIBITION
sections.text:
•Any substance that can diminish the velocity of enzyme-catalyzed reaction is called an inhibitor.
•Enzyme inhibition can be either reversible or irreversible.

sections.heading:
A REVERSIBLE ENZYME INHIBITION
05 ENZYME INHIBITION

1 Competitive Inhibitors (Substrate analogue inhibitors
05 ENZYME INHIBITION › A REVERSIBLE ENZYME INHIBITION
sections.text:
•A competitive inhibitor is structurally similar to the of substrate.
•Hence, it competes with the substrate to bind reversibly to the active site.
•Thus, the degree of inhibition depends on ratio of concentration of inhibitor to that of the substrate and not on the absolute concentration of either of them.
•Degree of inhibition also depends on relative affinity of substrate & inhibitor to enzyme.
•Effect on Vmaxand Km:
▪No effect on Vmax: The effect of a competitive inhibitor is reversed by increasing [S] At a sufficiently high substrate concentration.
▪the reaction velocity reaches the same Vmaxobserved in the absence of inhibitor.
▪Kmincreases: A competitive inhibitor increases apparent Kmfor a given substrate.
▪This means that, in the presence of a competitive inhibitor ,more substrate is needed to achieve ½Vm.

sections.heading:
2 Allosteric Inhibitors
05 ENZYME INHIBITION › A REVERSIBLE ENZYME INHIBITION
sections.text:
•They are small organic molecules that bind to a specific site away from the active site.
•They produce conformational changes in enzyme structure that lead to decreased activity of the enzyme e.g., ATP for phosphofructokinase-1.
•Effect on Vmax and Km:

▪Vmax decreases: because they decrease the maximal catalytic activity.
▪Km increases: because they decrease the affinity of the enzyme to its substrate.
•Feedback Inhibition:
▪It is the inhibition of the activity of an enzyme in a pathway by the end products of this pathway.
▪Occurs through binding of end product to allosteric site present on key enzyme.
▪This usually occurs at the earliest irreversible step unique to that pathway.
▪This prevents accumulation of unwanted amounts of metabolic end products.

•In the case of branched biosynthetic pathways, multiple feedback loops are more common for regulation of the enzymes of these pathways.

•In this model each of P1 and P2 produces feedback inhibition of a specific enzyme in its biosynthesis i.e. Enz-4 and 5 respectively.
•At the same time both produce inhibition of Enz-l (Common for both biosynthetic pathways)
•The inhibition of one enzyme by two or more products is additive as the enzyme contains more than one allosteric site (Cumulative feedback inhibition).

sections.heading:
1 Inhibitors of cofactors (non-protein part)
05 ENZYME INHIBITION › B IRREVERSIBLE ENZYME INHIBITION
sections.text:
1Fluoride:
•Blocks the action of enzymes
•It require Ca+2& Mg+2ions by chelating these ions in the form of salts
•Example: Chelation of Mg+2in case of enolase (An enzyme of glucose oxidation), thus inhibiting the enzyme.
2Cyanide & carbon monoxide:
•Inhibit the activity of cytochrome oxidase, an enzyme of the respiratory chain, by blocking the iron of heme.

sections.heading:
2 Inhibitors of the apoenzyme (Protein part)
05 ENZYME INHIBITION › B IRREVERSIBLE ENZYME INHIBITION
sections.text:
•These are inhibitors that either denature proteins or block chemical groups which are important for substrate binding and/ or catalysis.
1Antienzymes
▪They are specific to enzymes that bind with them and produce their inactivation
▪As antithrombin binds to thrombin and inhibits blood clotting.
2Inhibitors that denature proteins
▪These include strong acids, alkalis, alcohols, and salts of heavy metals.
3Inhibitors that block chemical groups (enzyme poisons)
▪Inhibitors of the sulfhydryl groups
▸The presence of free SH groups is important for the catalytic activity of many enzymes.
▸These inhibitors act by binding to or modifying the SH groups thus impairing enzyme function as in arsenic poisoning.
▪Inhibitors that block hydroxyl groups
▸Aspirin produces acetylation of the hydroxyl group of serine at the active site of cyclooxygenase enzyme (Responsible for prostaglandin synthesis), explaining the anti-inflammatory and antipyretic actions of aspirin.

sections.heading:
A ALLOSTERIC ACTIVATORS
06 ENZYME ACTIVATION
sections.text:
•The binding of an allosteric activator with the allosteric site produces conformational changes in the protein structure of the enzyme, which result in ↑↑ velocity of the reaction.
•Allosteric activator increases affinity of the enzyme to its substrate (Decrease Kmvalue) and increases the maximal catalytic activity (Increase Vmax).
•Many cellular metabolic reactions are controlled in this way e.g:
▪AMP acts as an allosteric activator for the phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).

sections.heading:
B ACTIVATION OF PROENZYMES (ZYMOGENS)
06 ENZYME ACTIVATION
sections.text:
•Many enzymes are formed as proenzymes which are inactive.
•Activation requires proteolysis (Removal of a part of the polypeptide chain which masks the active site or substrate site).
•A good example is the formation of digestive proteolytic enzymes as zymogens inside the cells to prevent digestion of cellular proteins.
•When these zymogens are released into the gut, they are activated to digest food proteins
•Many of these enzymes after activation can activate their zymogens in a process termed autocatalytic activation (Autocatalysis).

sections.heading: 07 COVALENT MODIFICATIONS
sections.text:
•Reversible Phosphorylation / Dephosphorylation :
▪Many enzymes are activated by phosphorylation and inactivated by dephosphorylation and vice versa.
▪This means that the enzyme is present in two interconvertible forms (Phosphorylated & dephosphorylated).
▪The phosphate groups are usually attached to the hydroxyl group of amino acids (Mainly serine or tyrosine) present in the polypeptide chain of the enzyme.

sections.heading: 01 HEMOPROTEINS
sections.text:
•These are conjugated proteins, containing heme as a “prosthetic group”.
•A prosthetic group is a tightly bound non-protein molecule that does not dissociate from the protein and is essential for its biological activity.

sections.heading: 02 CHEMISTRY OF HEME
sections.text:
•Heme is a ferrous (Fe+2) protoporphyrin IX.
•Protoporphyrins contain the porphin ring.
•Porphin ring is formed of four pyrrole rings linked through methenyl bridges.
•The four pyrrole rings are labeled I, II, III, and IV.
•Substituent positions on the rings are labeled 7 ,6 ,5 ,4 ,3 ,2 ,1 and 8.
•The methenyl bridges are labeled β, α, γ and δ.
•The chemical groups attached to porphin ring are of two types:
▪Non-polar groups: four methyl groups (M) and Two vinyl groups (V).
▪Polar groups: Two propionate groups (P).
•The ferrous iron (Fe+2) is held in the center of the heme molecule by bonds with four nitrogen atoms of the porphin ring.

sections.heading: 03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Both conjugated proteins are formed of heme attached to a basic protein i.e., apomyoglobin in myoglobin and globin in hemoglobin.
•Myoglobin is formed of one heme attached to one polypeptide chain, while hemoglobin is formed of four heme groups attached to four polypeptide chains.

sections.heading:
A GENERAL CHARACHTERS
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Site
▪Myoglobin is present in cardiac and skeletal muscles.
•Function
▪It functions in both tissues as a reservoir for oxygen, and as an oxygen carrier that increases the rate of release of oxygen within the muscle cell during severe muscular exercise when the partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) is reduced to 5mmHg.
•Affinity to oxygen
▪Myoglobin has a greater affinity to oxygen than hemoglobin, myoglobin is 90% saturated at pO220mmHg

sections.heading:
1 The protein part (Apomyoglobin)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › B STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•Primary structure:
▪The protein contains 153 amino acids, forming a single polypeptide chain.
•Secondary structure:
▪The chain is folded into eight α-helices named A, B, C, D, E, F, G & H starting from the N -terminal end.
▪Every amino acid is given a letter to determine its helix and a number to localize its position from the N-terminal end of that helix e.g., His E7 is the amino acid number 7 at the E helix.
▪The loops in between the helices are given the letters of the two helices they connect e.g., EF connects the helix E with F
•Tertiary structure
▪Apomyoglobin is further folded to form a globular protein with the polar amino acids toward the surface (So it is water soluble)
▪The nonpolar amino acids at the inner part except for the two amino acids histidine F8 and histidine E7 that have a role in oxygen binding.

sections.heading:
2 The Heme ring
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › B STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•It is present inside the hydrophobic core of apomyoglobin polypeptide chain in a pocket between E and F helices.
•Heme interacts with the chain through:
▪Hydrophobic bonds between its nonpolar side chains and the nonpolar amino acids of the apomyoglobin chain.
▪Its iron that interacts with the

proximal histidine.

sections.heading:
C INTERACTION OF IRON WITH HEME AND APOMYOGLOBIN
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Iron in the ferrous state (Fe II) can form 6 coordinate bonds:
▪Four coordinations are formed between Fe II and the four nitrogen atoms of the porphyrin ring, which lie in the same plane of the ring.
▪The fifth coordination is for the proximal histidine (His F8)
▪The sixth coordination is for oxygen.
▪The latter lies between Fe II & another molecule of histidine termed distal histidine (His E7).
▪It is unoccupied in the absence of O2.
▪Both the 5th& 6thco-ordinations lie in an axis perpendicular to plane of porphyrin ring.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › C INTERACTION OF IRON WITH HEME AND APOMYOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Myoglobin is present in cardiac and skeletal muscles.
•During heart attack or severe muscle damage, myoglobin is released into blood .
•It increases in blood 2 to 3 hours after the first symptoms of muscle damage and usually peaks about 8 to 12 hours later.

sections.heading:
A GENERAL CHARACHTERS
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Site
▪Hemoglobin (Hb) is found exclusively in red blood cells
•Function
▪Transport oxygen from the lungs to all tissues.
▪Transports CO₂ and H⁺ back to lungs.
▪The oxy Hb/Hb system acts as a buffer in the RBCs.

sections.heading:
B STRUCTURE
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Hemoglobin structure during embryonic and fetal life differs from adulthemoglobin.
•All are tetramers formed of different types of polypeptide chains encoded by different genes

sections.heading:
1 Embryonic and Fetal Hemoglobin
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › B STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•Embryonic Hemoglobin (Hb Gower)
▪The first hemoglobin formed during the first few weeks after conception.
▪They include:
▸Hemoglobin Gower-1, consisting of two zeta and two epsilon chains (ζ2ε2).
▸Hemoglobin Gower-2, consisting of two alpha & two epsilon chains (α2ε2).
•Fetal hemoglobin (HbF)
▪It is formed at the 3rdmonth of pregnancy and remains up to 6 months after birth.
▪It consists of two alpha and two gamma chains (α2γ2).
▪It has higher affinity to O2than adult Hb to allow more efficient transplacental transfer of oxygen from maternal to fetal hemoglobin

sections.heading:
2 AdultHemoglobin
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › B STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•It is formed at the end of the late month of pregnancy and continues throughout life.
•Adult Hb A1 (HbA1):
▪It forms about 98% of total adult Hb.
▪It consists of two alpha and two beta chains (α2β2)
•Adult Hb A2 (HbA2):
▪It forms only 2% of total adult Hb.
▪It consists of two alpha and two delta chains (δ2α2).

sections.heading:
Structure of Hemoglobin A1
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › B STRUCTURE › 2 AdultHemoglobin
sections.text:
(The major hemoglobin in adults)
•It is a tetramer composed of 4 polypeptide chains
▪2 identical α-chains
▪2 identical β-chains
•Each chain binds with one heme ring

sections.heading:
THE PROTEIN PART (GLOBIN)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Primary structure:
▪Each α-chain has 7 helices, while each β-chain has 8 helices.
▪The names of the helices, the amino acids, and the loops between the helices are similar to those of apomyoglobin.
•Secondary structure:
▪Each α-chain has 7 helices, while each β-chain has 8 helices.
▪The names of the helices, the amino acids, and the loops between the helices are similar to those of apomyoglobin.
•Tertiary structure:
▪Each chain is further folded to form a globular structure with the polar amino acids toward the surface, and the nonpolar amino acids at the inner part.
•Quaternary structure:
▪The 4 polypeptide chains interact together as follows:
▸Each (α) and (β) chain are held together forming two identical dimers (αβ)1and (αβ)2in which the numbers refer to dimers one and two.
▸The two chains within a dimer are held together by hydrophobic interactions which prevent their movement relative to each other.
▸However, the two dimers are linked with each other by non-covalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen and ionic bonds), so the two dimers can move freely during oxygenation and deoxygenation.

sections.heading:
HEME RINGS:
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text: •Each globin polypeptide chain binds with one heme ring in a similar manner to that described for myoglobin.

sections.heading:
1c
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › HEME RINGS:
sections.text:
•Hemoglobin A1c(HbA1c) (Glycated Hb):
▪Part of adult hemoglobin can bind with blood glucose forming glycated Hb or HbA1c.
▪Glucose forms a covalent bond with the (N-terminal valine of the β chain).
▪It is a non-enzymatic reaction that depends on the exposure of RBCs to certain blood glucose levels throughout the life span of RBCs (120 days).
▪HbA1c represents 4 to 5.7% of HbA in normal individuals.
▪Higher levels are present in cases of diabetes mellitus, and HbA1c is used as a test to determine the diabetic control of the patients during the last 3 months.

sections.heading:
C IMPORTANCE OF THE GLOBIN PROTEIN OF HEMOGLOBIN
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•Makes heme soluble:
▪Due to the presence of surface polar amino acids.
•Prevents iron oxidation:
▪It prevents the oxidation of heme into hematin (Due to the nonpolar amino acids lining of heme pocket).
▪Also, it prevents the formation of heme-O2-heme complex.
•Prevents diffusion of heme to plasma:
▪Due to its large size
•Reduces the affinity of heme to bind carbon monoxide (CO):
▪CO can bind to isolated heme in its preferred orientation i.e., with all three atoms (Fe, C, and O) perpendicular to the plane of the heme, while in myoglobin and hemoglobin the distal histidine sterically hinders this orientation.
▪Binding at a less favored angle reduces the strength of the heme-CO bond.

sections.heading:
D AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN TO OXYGEN
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text: 2 forms of Hb exist depending on presence or absence of oxygen

sections.heading:
1 T form
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › D AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN TO OXYGEN
sections.text:
•The deoxy form of hemoglobin is called the "T" (tense) form.
•In the T form, the two dimers interact through a network of ionic bonds & hydrogen bonds that constrain the movement of the polypeptide chains.
•The T form is the low oxygen-affinity form of hemoglobin.

sections.heading:
2 R form
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › D AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN TO OXYGEN
sections.text:
•The binding of oxygen to hemoglobin causes rupture of some of the noncovalent bonds between the two dimers, which allows the dimers to rotate ~15° relative to each other.
•This leads to a structure called the "R," or relaxed form, in which the polypeptide chains have more freedom of movement.
•The R form is the high oxygen-affinity form of hemoglobin.

sections.heading:
E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text:
•The ability of hemoglobin to perform its function is affected by:

▪O2(Heme-heme interactions)
▪Bohr effect (pH)

▪CO
▪CO2

▪2,3bisphosphoglycerate.

sections.heading:
1 Binding to oxygen (heme-heme interaction)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
sections.text:
•Although it is more difficult for the first oxygen molecule to bind to hemoglobin
•The subsequent binding of oxygen occurs with high affinity.
•The net effect is that affinity of hemoglobin for the last oxygen bound is approximately 300 times greater than its affinity for the first oxygen bound.
•The cooperative binding of oxygen enhances the efficiency of hemoglobin as an oxygen transporter.

sections.heading:
2 Bohr effect (pH)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
sections.text:
•Bohr effect is a physiological phenomenon that explains how hemoglobin's oxygen binding affinity is inversely related both to acidity (High proton concentration) and to the concentration of carbon dioxide.
•At the tissues:
▪Carbon dioxide generated in peripheral tissues combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into protons and bicarbonate ions.
▪Protons are added to the N-terminal amino groups of the imidazole rings of histidine 146 in the β chain in Hb stabilizing the T-form.
▪The affinity of Hb to O2decreases, which helps the release of O2to tissues.
•At the lungs:
▪The reverse occurs and CO2is lost.The binding of O2to Hb releases 2 protons.
▪The liberated hydrogen ions combine with bicarbonate, forming carbonic acid, which is broken by carbonic anhydrase to CO2and water; then CO2is lost through the lungs.

sections.heading:
3 Binding to carbon monoxide (Carboxyhemoglobin)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
sections.text:
•Carbon monoxide (CO) binds tightly (but reversibly) to hemoglobin iron, forming carboxyhemoglobin.
•When CO binds to one or more of the four heme sites, hemoglobin shifts to the relaxed conformation, causing the remaining heme bind oxygen with high affinity.
•As a result, the affected hemoglobin is unable to release oxygen to the tissues.
•Since, affinity of hemoglobin for CO is about 200 times greater than for oxygen, as a result even minute concentrations of CO in the environment can produce toxic concentrations of carboxyhemoglobin in the blood.
•Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with 100 percent oxygen therapy, which facilitates the dissociation of CO from hemoglobin.

sections.heading:
4 Binding to carbon dioxide (carbamino-hemoglobin)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
sections.text:
•Most of the carbon dioxide molecules produced in metabolism are hydrated by carbonic anhydrase enzyme and transported as “Bicarbonate ions”.
•However, some CO2is carried as carbamate bound to the uncharged α-amino groups of hemoglobin as “Carbamino-hemoglobin”, as follows:

•At tissues, carbamino-hemoglobin with its negative charge stabilizes the T or deoxy form of hemoglobin, resulting in a decrease of its affinity for oxygen and thus helping the release of oxygen.

sections.heading:
5 Binding to -2,3Bisphosphoglycerate (-2,3BPG)
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › E FACTORS AFFECTING THE AFFINITY OF HEMOGLOBIN FOR OXYGEN
sections.text:
•2,3-BPG is a by-product of glycolysis in red blood cells that reduces hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen.
•One molecule of 2,3-BPG binds to a pocket, formed by the two β-globin chains, in the center of the deoxyhemoglobin.
•This pocket contains several positively charged amino acid side chains that form ionic bonds with the negatively charged groups of 2,3-BPG.
•Binding favors T form reducing the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen and helps the release of oxygen to the tissues.
•At the lungs, O2binds to Hb; the pocket becomes small and BPG slips out.
•This favors R form and helps oxygenation.

sections.heading:
F ORGANIZATION OF GLOBIN GENES
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
sections.text: •The globin genes, which direct the synthesis of the different globin chains, are structurally organized into gene families located on two different chromosomes.

sections.heading:
1 α-Gene family
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › F ORGANIZATION OF GLOBIN GENES
sections.text:
•The α-gene cluster on chromosome 16 contains:
▪Two genes for the α-globin chains (α1 & α2).
▪The zeta gene

sections.heading:
2 β- Gene family
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN › F ORGANIZATION OF GLOBIN GENES
sections.text:
•The β-gene cluster on chromosome 11 contains:
▪The single β-gene that encodes the β-chain.
▪Additional four genes:
1The epsilon (ε) gene is expressed early in embryonic development.
2The δ gene that codes for globin chain is found in minor adult hemoglobin HbA2.
3Two γ-genes which are expressed in fetal hemoglobin.

sections.heading:
G MAIN DIFFERENCES BETWEEN MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN A1
03 MYOGLOBIN AND HEMOGLOBIN
04 HEMOGLOBINOPATHIES
sections.text:
•Hemoglobinopathies are family of disorders caused by synthesis of:
▪Structurally abnormal globin chains, e.g., Sickle-cell anemia (HbS)
▪Abnormal reduced amount of α- or β- globin chains, e.g., thalassemias

sections.heading:
A SICKLE CELL ANEMIA
04 HEMOGLOBINOPATHIES
sections.text:
•It is a genetic disorder common among black populations all over the world.
•Cause:
▪It is caused by a single nucleotide alteration (Point mutation) in the β-globin gene, leading to replacement of polar glutamate at position six with a nonpolar valine.
•Mechanism and consequences of sickling:
▪The nonpolar amino acid generates a hydrophobic “Sticky patch” on the surface of the β subunit of both oxy-HbS and deoxy-HbS.
▪Both HbA and HbS contain a complementary hydrophobic “Sticky receptor” on the β subunits only in the deoxygenated state.
▪Thus, at low pO2, deoxy-HbS molecules can polymerize and form long insoluble fibers that distort the RBCs cytoskeleton and push against their membrane giving them the crescent (Sickle) shape.
▪Such sickled cells frequently block the flow of blood in the narrow capillaries leading to localized anoxia (Oxygen deprivation) in the tissue, causing pain and eventually death (Infarction) of the cells near the blockage.
▪The spleen removes sickle cells at a faster rate than normal cells (Shorter life span), leading to hemolytic anemia.

sections.heading:
B THALASSEMIA
04 HEMOGLOBINOPATHIES
sections.text:
•Thalassemia is a hereditary disease in which there is defective production of either α-chain (α-thalassemia) or the β- chain (β-thalassemia).
•Severity of disease depends on number of genes affected & the symptoms vary from very mild to severe anemia and even death of the fetus before birth or immediately after birth.

sections.heading: 05 METABOLISM OF HEME

A SITE
05 METABOLISM OF HEME
sections.text:
•Organ site:
▪The erythrocyte-producing cells of the bone marrow.
▪The liver.
•Intracellular site:
▪Some steps in the mitochondria and others in the cytosol.

sections.heading:
1 Formation of δ-aminolevulinate (In mitochondria):
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•It is formed by condensation of glycine & succinyl-CoA catalyzed by δ-aminolevulinate synthase (ALA synthase), which is the key regulatory enzyme of the heme biosynthetic pathway.
•This enzyme needs pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a coenzyme.
•PLP is the active form of vitamin B6.
•ALA synthase is allosterically inhibited by heme (End-product feedback inhibition).
•Heme also represses the synthesis of ALA synthase.

sections.heading:
2 Formation of porphobilinogen (PBG) (In cytosol)
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•Two molecules of ALA condense forming porphobilinogen (PBG) catalyzed by δ-aminolevulinate dehydratase (ALA dehydratase).
•This enzyme is inhibited by lead in cases of lead poisoning.

sections.heading:
3 Formation of hydroxymethylbilane (In cytosol)
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text: •Four PBG molecules condense to form a linear tetrapyrrole (hydroxymethylbilane), by the enzyme uroporphyrinogen I synthase.

sections.heading:
4 Formation of uroporphyrinogen III (In cytosol)
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text: •Hydroxymethylbilane cyclizes to form uroporphyrinogen III by uroporphyrinogen III synthase.

sections.heading:
5 Formation of coproporphyrinogen III (In cytosol)
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text: •The 4 acetate side chains (A) of uroporphyrinogen III are converted to 4 methyl groups (M) by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

sections.heading:
6 Formation of heme (In mitochondria)
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•Subsequent reactions by specific oxidases lead to formation of protoporphyrin IX.
•Insertion of the ferrous iron into the center of the protoporphyrin ring catalyzed by ferrochelatase (Heme synthase) to form heme.
•Ferrochelatase is inhibited by lead.

sections.heading:
Note !!
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B MAIN STEPS OF HEME SYNTHESIS › 6 Formation of heme (In mitochondria)
sections.text:
•In lead poisoning, lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase enzyme

•Porphyrias are caused by inherited (or occasionally acquired) defects in heme synthesis
•Resulting in the accumulation of porphyrins or porphyrin precursors in the tissues and their increased excretion in urine.
•Two types of clinical manifestations can be observed in porphyrias:

sections.heading:
A NEUROPSYCHIATRIC MANIFESTATION (ACUTE PORPHYRIA):
05 METABOLISM OF HEME
sections.text:
•These are characterized by the accumulation of ALA or PBG, because of relative or absolute inhibition of the enzymes ALA dehydratase or uroporphyrinogen I synthase, together with increased activity of the enzyme ALA synthase.
•ALA and PBG are neurotoxic (Decrease ATPase activity in nerve cells)
▪They cause injury to sympathetic nerves (Abdominal pain)
▪Also to somatic nerves (Peripheral neuritis, skeletal muscle paralysis & neuropsychiatric symptoms).
•This explains the neuropsychiatric symptoms that occur in acute porphyria.
•E.g.: Acute intermittent porphyria (Uroporphyrinogen I synthase deficiency).

sections.heading:
B PHOTOSENSITIVITY
05 METABOLISM OF HEME
sections.text:
•Any enzyme defect after synthesis of the porphyrinogen ring will lead to the accumulation of porphyrinogens in the skin, which will be spontaneously oxidized to porphyrins.
•Porphyrins absorb light, particularly at a wavelength of 400 nm.
•This activates porphyrins to release free radicals that cause damage to lysosomes which release lysosomal enzymes thatdestroy skin cells.
•Thus, exposure to light leads to skin damage and scarring.
•E.g.: Porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency).

sections.heading:
Note !!
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B PHOTOSENSITIVITY
sections.text:
•Many drugs can precipitate acute attacks of porphyria as they induce ALA synthase
•E.g.: Barbiturates, estrogens and sulfonamides

•A Human turns over approximately 6 g of hemoglobin per day.
•It is estimated that 1 g of hemoglobin yields 35 mg of bilirubin.
•The formation of the bilirubin occurs subsequently in:

sections.heading:
1 Reticuloendothelial System
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B PHOTOSENSITIVITY
sections.text:
•After approximately 120 days in the circulation, the erythrocytes are taken up by the reticuloendothelial cells, Where the hemoglobin becomes liberated.
•Globin is removed and undergoes proteolysis into amino acids.
•The first step in the degradation of heme is catalyzed by the heme oxygenase system of the RE cells in the presence of NADPH and O2.
•Ferric iron & carbon monoxide are released, resulting in production of green pigment biliverdin.
•Biliverdin (Green) becomes reduced to bilirubin (Yellow) by biliverdin reductase.
•Bilirubin is slightly soluble in plasma; therefore, it is transported in blood carried on albumin.
•It is the chief bilirubin in the blood, hence the name (Hemobilirubin), which is also called “Unconjugated bilirubin”. It cannot be excreted in urine.
•If the plasma level of this bilirubin exceeds the carrying capacity of albumin (About 20 mg/dL), it passes the blood brain barrier (Due to its hydrophobic nature) & produces brain damage or “Kernicterus”.

sections.heading:
2 Liver
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B PHOTOSENSITIVITY
sections.text:
•Unconjugated bilirubin is taken up by liver cells, where bilirubin dissociates from albumin.
•Conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid is catalyzed by enzyme glucuronyltransferase.
•This type of bilirubin is called “Conjugated bilirubin”.
•Conjugation increases polarity and water-solubility of bilirubin.
•Glucuronylansferase is induced by certain drugs, e.g., phenobarbital, and by glucose.
•Excretion of conjugated bilirubin is principally through bile & hence name “Cholebilirubin”.
•Only traces go back to the blood.
•Being water-soluble, conjugated bilirubin is not bound to plasma proteins; thus, it can be excreted in urine but does not pass the blood brain barrier.

sections.heading:
3 Intestines
05 METABOLISM OF HEME › B PHOTOSENSITIVITY
sections.text:
•In the large intestine, by action of enzymes derived from intestinal bacterial flora, bilirubin is released from glucuronic acid & undergoes successive reductions ending in the formation of stercobilinogen.
•The colorless stercobilinogen may have several fates:
▪The majority are excreted in stools and spontaneously oxidized by the oxygen of air to brown stercobilin, which gives stool its brown color.
▪About 10% is absorbed from the intestines and returned, via portal blood, to the liver to be excreted again in bile “Enterohepatic circulation”.
▪Very little amount normally escapes to the systemic circulation then to the kidneys as colorless urobilinogen where it is converted to yellowurobilin on exposure to air, which gives urine its normal color.

sections.heading: 06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN
sections.text:
•Serum bilirubin can be estimated by the Van den Bergh reaction, in which the bilirubin is coupled with a certain reagent to yield a violet dye.
•The water-soluble conjugated bilirubin (As it is not bound to proteins) reacts rapidly with the reagent (Within one minute) and is said to be “Direct reacting.”
•The less soluble unconjugated bilirubin (It is bound to albumin) reacts after the addition of solvent like methanol.
•Unconjugated bilirubin becomes soluble, and both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin react with the reagent, providing the “Total bilirubin” value.
•The indirect-reacting bilirubin, which corresponds to the unconjugated bilirubin, is obtained by subtracting the direct-reacting bilirubin from the total bilirubin.
•Normally:
▪Total serum bilirubin range 0.2-1.2 mg/dL
▪Indirect bilirubin range 0.2-0.9 mg/dL
▪Direct bilirubin < 0.3 mg/dL

•Definition:
▪Jaundice refers to the yellow discoloration of skin, nails, and sclerae due to elevation of serum bilirubin above 2 mg/dL.
•Classification:
▪According to the predominant form of bilirubin in serum, jaundice is classified into:
▸Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
▸Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
▸Both unconjugated and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (mixed type).

sections.heading:
1 Hemolytic jaundice
06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN › A UNCONJUGATEDHYPERBILIRUBINEMIA
sections.text:
•In hemolytic jaundice, there is increased hemolysis, leading to increased production of bilirubin beyond the excretory capacity of the liver.
•Serum bilirubin increases, mainly unconjugated bilirubin.
•Stercobilin increases in feces, which becomes dark brown.
•Since unconjugated bilirubin is bound to the plasma albumin, it cannot be excreted in the urine, and hence the name “Acholuric jaundice”.
•Some causes of hemolytic jaundice include:
▪Abnormal hemoglobin: Sickle cell anemia and thalassemias.
▪Red cell enzymes deficiency: Glucose-6-P dehydrogenase (G6PD) & pyruvate kinase.
▪Red cell antibodies: Incompatible blood transfusion & erythroblastosis fetalis.
▪Some infections e.g., malaria.

sections.heading:
2 Physiological neonatal jaundice
06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN › A UNCONJUGATEDHYPERBILIRUBINEMIA
sections.text:
•It is a transient condition that occurs in the first few days of life.
•It results partly from increased hemolysis and partly from immaturity of the enzyme UDP-glucuronyltransferase.
•Serum bilirubin usually does not reach 13 mg/dL.
•Treatment:
▪Exposure to blue, fluorescent light (Phototherapy) helps conversion of insoluble form of unconjugated bilirubin to the more soluble photoisomers that can be excreted into the bile without conjugation to glucuronic acid.
▪Phenobarbital may also be used in the treatment of these cases to induce the synthesis of the enzyme glucuronyltransferase

sections.heading:
3 Gilbert Syndrome
06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN › A UNCONJUGATEDHYPERBILIRUBINEMIA
sections.text:
•A benign condition caused by a defect in the uptake of unconjugated bilirubin by the liver and conjugation pathways.
•Newborns have mildhyperbilirubinemia.

sections.heading:
B CONJUGATED HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA (OBSTRUCTIVE JAUNDICE)
06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN
sections.text:
•This is caused by obstruction of the biliary passages, e.g., by gallstones, cancer head of pancreas or inflammation of the pancreas or of the biliary passages.
•This leads to regurgitation of conjugated bilirubin to the blood.
•Serum bilirubin increases mainly conjugated bilirubin.
•Stercobilin disappears from the feces leading to clay colored stool.
•Conjugated bilirubin becomes excreted in the urine, which becomes dark brown in color.
•The urine also contains bile salts.
•Due to biliary obstruction, serum level of the enzyme alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is elevated.

sections.heading:
C BOTH CONJUGATED & UNCONJUGATED HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA
06 BLOOD BILIRUBIN
sections.text:
•This is also called toxic hyperbilirubinemia or hepatocellular jaundice.
•It is usually due to:
▪Viral hepatitis
▪May also be caused by some toxins as paracetamol and chloroform.
•Liver capacity to conjugate bilirubin decreases, leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
•In addition, liver cells usually swell and block the biliary canaliculi, leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
•Stercobilin in the feces usually decreases (Faint stool).
•conjugated bilirubin appears in the urine, which becomes dark brown in color.
•Due to liver cell damage, the serum levels of the enzymes Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) are elevated.
