sections.heading: 01 INTRO.TO PROTEINS OF EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX
sections.text:
•The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a major component of the connective tissues(CT) that surround and support the tissues and organs.
•Connective tissue is made up of:
▪Cells: e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, mesenchymal cells, chondrocytes and osteocytes.
▪Extracellular matrix: is made up of
▸Fibrous proteins: Collagen, elastin, fibrillin, fibronectin and laminin.
▸Proteoglycans: A core of proteins (5%) attached to glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)
▸Water
▸Minerals

sections.heading: 02 COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•It is a fibrous protein & is the most abundant protein in body (Forms 25% of total body proteins).
•It is present & has supportive function in:
▪Tendons, skin, cartilage, bones, lungs, liver, vessels, & cornea.
•It is synthesized by fibroblasts, mesenchymal cells, chondrocytes, and osteocytes.

sections.heading:
1 Tropocollagen molecule
02 COLLAGEN › A STRUCTURE OF COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•It is the building unit of collagen which consists of three coiled α-chains.
•Each α-chain is coiled in a left-handed helix.
•The presence of prolineprevents right-handed helix formation.
•The three left-handed α-chains are tightly twisted to form a right-handed superhelix (Tropocollagen molecule).

sections.heading:
2 Amino acid composition
02 COLLAGEN › A STRUCTURE OF COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•Each α-chain contains approximately 1000 amino acids having the repeating triplet sequence Gly-X-Y.
•Where Gly is glycine (Present in every third position), X is Proline & Y is hydroxyproline.
•The X position is sometimes occupied by lysine
•The Y position is sometimes occupied by hydroxylysine.
•Different types of collagens vary in number of hydroxylysine residues.
•Glucose & galactose molecules are attached to hydroxylysine residues (so collagen is considered as a glycoprotein)

sections.heading:
B TYPES OF COLLAGENS
02 COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•The collagen superfamily includes more than twenty collagen types.
•The most common types are type I and type II:
▪Type I contains two identical α1 chains and one α2 chain (α1)2(α2)
▪Type II collagen contains three identical α1 chains (α1)3

sections.heading:
1 Intracellular Steps
02 COLLAGEN › C SYNTHESIS OF COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•Synthesis of preprocollagen α-chain :
▪It is formed on the rough endoplasmic reticulum .
▪Preprocollagen chain has one N-terminal signal peptide & two extension peptides (One at each terminus).
•Conversion of preprocollagen α-chain to procollagen α-chain:
▪Removal of the signal peptide .
▪Hydroxylation of some proline and lysine residues by hydroxylase enzymes (Require vitamin C as cofactor).
▪Glycosylation of some hydroxylysine residues by adding glucose or galactose.
•Formation of triple helix procollagen molecule :
▪3 procollagen α-chains adhere to form the triple helix procollagen molecule by:
▸Formation of disulfide bonds in C-terminal extension peptides by oxidation of cysteine residues .
▸Folding to form the triple helix.
•Secretion:
▪The procollagen molecules are secreted into extracellular space by exocytosis.

sections.heading:
2 Extracellular Steps
02 COLLAGEN › C SYNTHESIS OF COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•Formation of tropocollagen molecule:
▪By removal of the two extension peptides from the N- & C-terminals by procollagen peptidases.
•Formation of collagen fibrils and fibers:
▪Tropocollagen molecules are assembled in a parallel and staggered array into collagen fibrils that are stabilized by covalent cross-links.
▪Collagen fibrils are then packed together to form collagen fibers which are further stabilized by the formation of more covalent cross-links

sections.heading:
Note !!
02 COLLAGEN › C SYNTHESIS OF COLLAGEN › 2 Extracellular Steps
sections.text: •The cross-links increase with age and collagen becomes less flexiblebarbiturates, estrogens and sulfonamides).

sections.heading:
1 Factors enhancing collagen production:
02 COLLAGEN › C FACTORS AFFECTING COLLAGEN PRODUCTION
sections.text:
•Vitamin C:
▪Essential for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues.
•Vitamin A:
▪Regulates collagen gene expression and promotes collagen synthesis.
•Adequate protein intake:
▪Provides necessary amino acids

sections.heading:
2 Factors reducing collagen production:
02 COLLAGEN › C FACTORS AFFECTING COLLAGEN PRODUCTION
sections.text:
•Smoking and excessive exposure to UV rays:
▪Reduce collagen production
▪Accelerate collagen degradation
•Aging:
▪As the body ages, collagen production naturally declines

sections.heading:
D COLLAGEN HAS A STRONG STRUCTURE DUE TO
02 COLLAGEN
sections.text:
•Each turn contains 3 amino acid residues (Makes a tight helix), while most of helical proteins contain 3.6 AAs per turn.
•The presence of glycine with its short side chain makes polypeptide chains very close to each other.
•The 3 left-handed coiled peptide chains form a right-handed superhelix.
•High content of hydroxyproline promotes more formation of interchainhydrogen bonds.
•The formation of covalent cross linkages between adjacent polypeptide chains is responsible for tensile properties of collagen (Stretched without being broken).
•The staggered array (Overhanging) gives marked flexibility to collagen.
•The specific arrangement into fibril and fibers.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
02 COLLAGEN › D COLLAGEN HAS A STRONG STRUCTURE DUE TO
sections.text:
•Scurvy:
▪Vitamin C deficiency leads to defective hydroxylation of collagen and thus production of weak collagen bleeding gums, poor wound healing….etc. (see vitamins).
•Ehlers-Danlos syndrome:
▪Defective formation of the covalent cross-links stretchable skin, hypermobile joints, and short stature.
•Osteogenesis imperfecta:
▪Mutation of collagen gene in which glycine residues are replaced by bulky amino acids, preventing the correct folding of the collagen chains into a triple helix and their assembly to form collagen fibrils.
▪This disease is known as “Brittle bone syndrome” manifested with deformed easily fractured bones, slight spinal curvature, loose joints, and poor muscle tone.

sections.heading: 03 ELASTIN
sections.text:
•It is a rubber like protein.
•It is present in elastic CT of ligaments, lungs, & walls of blood vessels.
•Structure of Elastin:
▪Tropoelastin is the building unit of elastin.
▪Tropoelastin is a monomer (One polypeptide chain) rich in lysine.
▪Some of lysyl residues of tropoelastin are converted by lysyl oxidase enzyme to allysin.
▪Three allysine plus one unmodified lysine form desmosine cross-link.
▪This makes elastin extensively interconnected and has rubbery network that can stretch and bend in any direction, giving connective tissue its elasticity.
▪Elastin is fibrous when stretched, globular when relaxed.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
03 ELASTIN
sections.text:
•Alpha1- Antitrypsin (AAT) Deficiency
▪AAT protein is produced by the liver, and protects tissues from elastase enzymes produced by inflammatory cells, especially neutrophils.
▪AAT deficiency is a hereditary disorder causing low levels of this protective protein, thus allowing elastase of neutrophil to break down elastin of the lungs, liver, skin and blood vessels.
▪Loss of elasticity of the lungs, producing respiratory complications such as emphysema, or COPD (Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).
▪The liver produces abnormal, misfolded AAT protein that gets stuck in the liver cells, causing liver damage and cirrhosis

sections.heading:
A DEFINITION
01 INTRODUCTION TO CARBOHYDRATES
sections.text:
•Carbohydrates are poly-hydroxy-alcohols with an aldehyde or keto group.
•Represented with a general formula Cn(H2O)n & hence are called hydrates of carbon.

sections.heading:
B IMPORTANCE
01 INTRODUCTION TO CARBOHYDRATES
sections.text:
•Providing a significant fraction of the dietary calories for energy production.
•Acting as a storage form of energy in the body.
•Serving as structural components on their own or combined with other molecules.

sections.heading:
C CLASSIFICATION
01 INTRODUCTION TO CARBOHYDRATES
sections.text:
•CHO are classified according to their hydrolysis products into 4 main groups:
▪Monosaccharides: consist of one monosaccharide unit.
▪Disaccharides: consist of 2 monosaccharide units per molecule.
▪Oligosaccharides: consist of 3 to 10 monosaccharide units per molecule.
▪Polysaccharides: consist of more than 10 monosaccharide units per molecule.

sections.heading: 02 MONOSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Monosaccharides are the simplest form of carbohydrates (Named simple sugars).
•They are classified according to:
▪Type of carbonyl group which may be an aldehyde group (Aldoses) or a ketone group (ketoses).
▪Number of carbons in the molecule into trioses (3 carbons), tetroses (4 carbons), pentoses (5 carbons), hexoses (6 carbons) and heptoses (7 carbons).

sections.heading:
1 Aldoses
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › A TYPES
sections.text: •Monosaccharides containing aldehyde group (H-C=O) at C1.

sections.heading:
2 Ketoses
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › A TYPES
sections.text:
•Monosaccharides containing ketone group (C=O) at C2.

•Cyclization of monosaccharides:
▪In solution, the functional group of the monosaccharide (aldehyde or ketone) combines with hydroxyl group of 5thcarbon atom forming a cyclic (ring) structure.

sections.heading:
B ISOMERISM OF MONOSACCHARIDES
02 MONOSACCHARIDES
sections.text: •Isomers are compounds which have the same molecular formula (the same number and types of atoms) but have different structural or steric formulae.

sections.heading:
1 Enantiomers
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › B ISOMERISM OF MONOSACCHARIDES
sections.text: •They are D- and L- forms of same compounds (mirror images) e.g.,D and L-glucose.

sections.heading:
2 Anomers
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › B ISOMERISM OF MONOSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Cyclization creates carbon atoms (C1 in aldose and C2 in ketoses) with two possible orientations of the hydroxyl group around it (α- and β-forms).
•The α-form has OH group to right (Down plane of the ring) of carbonyl carbon and the β- form has OH group to left (Above the plane of the ring) of carbonyl carbon.

sections.heading:
3 Aldose-Ketose Isomers (Functional Group Isomerism)
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › B ISOMERISM OF MONOSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•They have the same molecular formulae but differ in their functional groups.
•For example: (Fructose and glucose) and (Dihydroxy acetone and glyceraldehyde).
•Pentoses :

•Hexoses :
▪Glucose (Grape sugar):
▸The main sugar present in blood and is present in all animal and plant cells, honey & fruits.
▸It enters in the formation of many disaccharides and polysaccharides.
▪Fructose (Fruit sugar):
▸It is present in honey, fruits, semen, and sucrose.
▪Galactose:
▸It is a component of lactose (the milk sugar).
▸It is also found in glycosaminoglycans (GAGS), glycolipids and glycoproteins.

sections.heading:
1 Sugar acids
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › C MONOSACCHARIDE DERIVATIVES
sections.text:
•The most important sugar acids are “Uronic acids”, in which primary alcohol group of monosaccharides is oxidized to form corresponding uronic acid.
•For example: Glucose is oxidized to form glucuronic acid which has the following importance:
▪Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) synthesis (Aee later).
▪Conjugation reactions with many compounds to increase their water solubility to facilitate their urinary excretion.
▪Certain detoxification reactions.

sections.heading:
2 Sugar Alcohols
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › C MONOSACCHARIDE DERIVATIVES
sections.text:
•These are sugars in which the carbonyl group is reduced to an alcohol group.
•Important members of sugar alcohols:
1Glycerol:
▪It is glyceraldehyde or dihydroxyacetone alcohol.
▪It is a component of triacylglycerol and most phospholipids.
2Ribitol:
▪It is ribose alcohol.
▪It is a component of riboflavin (vitamin B2).
3Sorbitol:
▪It is glucose and fructose alcohol.
▪It is a natural product → might be involved in pathogenesis of diabetic complications.
▪It is also used as sweetener.
4Mannitol:
▪It is mannose alcohol.
▪It is used as a low-calorie sweetener as it is poorly absorbed by the intestin.
▪It increases plasma osmolality by drawing water from tissues into blood,
▪So mannitol is used clinically as a:
▸Diuretic by enhancing urine output and fluid excretion.
▸Treatment of glaucoma by reducing intraocular pressure.
▸Treatment of cerebral edema by lowering intracranial pressure.

sections.heading:
3 Deoxy sugars
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › C MONOSACCHARIDE DERIVATIVES
sections.text:
•These are sugars in which the hydroxyl group at C2 is replaced by a hydrogen atom.
•The most important example is the 2-Deoxy ribose which is present in structure of DNA.

sections.heading:
4 Amino sugars
02 MONOSACCHARIDES › C MONOSACCHARIDE DERIVATIVES
sections.text:
•These are sugars in which the hydroxyl group at C2 is replaced by an amino group (NH2)
•For example: glucosamine, galactosamine, and mannosamine.
•Amino sugars are important constituents of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and some types of glycolipids and glycoproteins.

sections.heading: 03 DISACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharides linked by glycosidic linkage.
•The glycosidic linkage is named according to:
▪The anomeric form (α or β).
▪The position of the connected carbons.
▪The sugar providing its anomeric carbon

sections.heading:
A MALTOSE (MALT SUGAR)
03 DISACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•It is formed of 2 molecules of glucose united by α 1,4-glucosidic linkage.
•Maltose is main product of digestion of starch by amylase.
•It is hydrolyzed by maltase enzyme or by acids into two molecules of D-glucose.

sections.heading:
B LACTOSE (MILK SUGAR)
03 DISACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•It is formed of galactose and glucose united by β1,4-galactosidic linkage.
•It is hydrolyzed by lactase enzyme or by acids into glucose and galactose.

sections.heading:
C SUCROSE (CANE OR TABLE SUGAR)
03 DISACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•It is present in plants as sugar cane and beets.
•Formed of Fructose & Glucose united by α1,2-glucosidic linkage or β1,2-fructosidic linkage.

sections.text:

sections.text:

•It is hydrolyzed by lactase enzyme or by acids into glucose and galactose.

sections.text:
•It is present in plants as sugar cane and beets.
•Formed of Fructose & Glucose united by α1,2-glucosidic linkage or β1,2-fructosidic linkage.

sections.heading: 04 POLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•They are composed of more than 10 monosaccharide units linked by glycosidic bonds.
•Polysaccharides are sub-classified into: Homopolysaccharides and Heteropolysaccharides.

sections.heading:
A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES
04 POLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•They are polysaccharides entirely made up of the same type of monosaccharide units.
•For example: starch, glycogen, and cellulose.

sections.heading:
1 Starch
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Starch is the chief storage form of carbohydrates in plants.
•It is present with large amounts in cereals (Rice and wheat), tubers (Potatoes & sweet potatoes) & legumes (Beans).
•Starch granules contain 2 forms, both present in same granule with different ratios:
▪Amylose: (20–30%) A linear polymer where glucose units are linked by α1,4-glucosidic bonds.
▪Amylopectin: (70–80%) A highly branched polymer containing both α1,4-glucosidic bonds for the main chain & α-1,6 glucosidic bonds at branching points.

sections.heading:
Note !!
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES › 1 Starch
sections.text:
•The ratio of amylose/amylopectin in starch granules affects digestibility, i.e. the higher the ratio, the slower the digestion and thus healthier effect.
•For example: Starch in short-grain rice has low ratio (~20:80 %), while starch in beans show higher ratio (~40:60) leading to slower digestion and healthier benefits.

sections.heading:
2 Glycogen
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Glycogen is the storage form of carbohydrates in animals.
•Present in most cells but especially in skeletal muscles & liver (As stores of excess glucose).
•It is a highly branched molecule (more branched than starch); glucose units are connected by α-1,4glucosidic bonds within the branches & α-1,6glucosidic bonds at branching points.

sections.heading:
3 Cellulose
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Cellulose forms the principal part of the cell wall of plants.
•Formed of a long non-branched chain of β-glucose units connected by β-1,4 glucosidic linkage.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › A HOMOPOLYSACCHARIDES › 3 Cellulose
sections.text:
•Cellulose in humans, as a key component of dietary fibers, is non-hydrolysable by amylase digestive enzyme because this enzyme hydrolyzes only α- linkages.
•Cellulose in diet is important in:
▪Preventing constipation as it increases bulk of stool → Stimulates intestinal contractions.
▪Delaying fat absorption.
▪Protecting against cancer colon.

sections.heading:
B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
04 POLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•These are polysaccharides which are formed of more than 1 type of monosaccharide unit.
•They include glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) that were formerly called mucopolysaccharides.

sections.heading:
1 Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Glycosaminoglycans are:
▪Unbranched
▪Long chains (Usually >50 sugar units) heteropolysaccharides
▪Mostly composed of repeating disaccharide units, each of which is made up of an amino sugar and a uronic acid.
•Glycosaminoglycans are classified into:
▪Sulfate free glycosaminoglycans: hyaluronic Acid
▪Sulfate containing glycosaminoglycans: chondroitin sulfate, keratan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, heparin and heparan sulfate.
•General properties of GAGs:
▪The negatively charged carboxylate & sulfate groups of GAGs help to trap water molecules
▪Thereby creating a hydrated gel with the following advantages:
1Provides flexible mechanical support for the extracellular matrix.
2Acts as a lubricant in synovial fluid.
3Acts as shock absorbent:
▸When a GAG solution is compressed, the water squeezed out & GAGs occupy a
smaller volume.
▸When compression is released,their molecules regain their original hydrated size.
▸This ex plains their role as shock absorbent in joints and making eyeball resilient.

sections.heading:
A Hyaluronic acid
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•It is distributed in many tissues and is abundant mainly in:
▪Skin: Aging is associated with reduced production of skin hyaluronic acid and collagen, with decrease in the formation of hydrating gel, causing loss of facial volume and the appearance of wrinkles.
▪Joints: In osteoarthritis, the concentration of hyaluronic acid gradually decreases, lowering the lubricant effect of synovial fluid.

sections.heading:
Hyaluronidase enzyme (Spreading factor)
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES › A Hyaluronic acid
sections.text:
•It can hydrolyze hyaluronic acid present in the ground substance of connective tissue.
•Hyaluronidase secreted by some bacteria helps spread of bacteria through subcutaneous tissues.
•It is present in sperms (heads) to help the process of ovum fertilization.

sections.heading:
B Chondroitin sulfate
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•It is the prominent component of cartilage, tendons, ligaments, bone, and aorta.
•It is commonly used as an oral treatment for osteoarthritis.

sections.heading:
C Keratan sulfate
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text: •It is one of the major components of the cornea and suggested to have important roles for corneal development and maintenance of its transparency.

sections.heading:
D Heparin
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Proteoglycan is an important anticoagulant (Prevents thrombus formation) by:
▪Inactivation of blood clotting factors IX and XI by binding to them.
▪Activation of antithrombin III by acting as a catalyst for it.
▪Also, Heparin helps in removal and clearance of blood lipids by binding to lipoprotein lipase enzyme and increasing its release from the capillary wall to the plasma.

sections.heading:
2 Proteoglycans
04 POLYSACCHARIDES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Most of the GAGs are covalently conjugated to a protein core, the product of which is termed proteoglycans.
•They are formed mainly of carbohydrates (%95) and only (%5) proteins.
•Proteoglycans are major constituents of extracellular matrix (ECM)
•They contribute to matrix organization & interact with structural proteins e.g. collagen & elastin.
•Aggrecan is the major proteoglycan present in cartilage.
•It has a very complex structure containing several types of GAGs (Hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfate & keratan sulfate) attached to a protein core and a link protein.
•It has a bottle brush shape.
•It is formed of a central long chain of hyaluronic acid attached to link proteins, which are attached to core proteins.
•Different types of GAGs project from these core proteins.

•Structure of aggrecan changes with age:
▪Keratan sulfate and protein contents increase.
▪Chondroitin sulfate content decreases.
▪Hyaluronic acid chain becomes shorter.
▪The average size decreases.
Thus, with age, cartilage compressibility will decrease, and human stature
will shorten.

01 INTRODUCTION TO LIPIDS
sections.text: •Lipids are hydrophobic organic compounds which are insoluble in water but soluble in fat solvents (Nonpolar solvents) e.g., benzene, alcohol, ether, chloroform, and acetone.

sections.heading:
B IMPORTANCE
01 INTRODUCTION TO LIPIDS
sections.text:
•Lipids provide the body with energy (9.3 kcal /gm).
•Supply body with fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids.
•Lipids inside the body have many biological functions (see later).

sections.heading: 02 FATTY ACIDS
sections.text:
•Fatty acids are monocarboxylic acids with hydrocarbon chains.
•They are the main components of all lipids

sections.heading:
A NOMENCLATURE
02 FATTY ACIDS
sections.text:
•The carboxyl carbon
▪It is carbon No. 1
▪The carbon atoms adjacent to it are numbered as 2 ,3 ,4…etc.
▪They are also known as α, β, γ…etc. carbons respectively.
•The terminal methyl group:
▪It is known as the ω1 carbon which is used to indicate the site of a double bond.
▪For example: ω3 indicates a double bond between 3rd& the 4thcarbons counting from the terminal methyl group.

sections.heading:
1 According to the Length of the Chain
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS
sections.text:
•Short chain fatty acids (from C2to C6)
•Medium chain fatty acids (from C8to C10)
•Long chain fatty acids (from C12to C22)
•Very long chain fatty acids (≥ C24)

sections.heading:

sections.text:
•Even chain fatty acids
•Odd chain fatty acids
Most naturally occurring fatty acids (> 95%) have an even number.

sections.heading:
A. Saturated Fatty Acids (SFA)
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS › 3 According to the Existence of Double Bonds
sections.text:
•They contain no double bonds.
•For example:

•The most important saturated fatty acids are palmitic and stearic acids
•They are widely distributed in animal fats.
•Sources:
▪Whole-milk, whole-milk products (cream, cheese, and butter), and fatty meats.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS › 3 According to the Existence of Double Bonds
sections.text: •Increased intake of saturated fatty acids may lead to an increase of plasma cholesterol levels that predispose to atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.

sections.heading:
B. Unsaturated Fatty Acids (USFA)
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS › 3 According to the Existence of Double Bonds
sections.text:
•They contain one or more double bonds
•Classified according to the orientation of hydrogen atoms around the double bond into cis fatty acids and trans fatty acids

1. Cis Fatty acids:
•Both hydrogen atoms are on the same side of the double bond.
•Fatty acids with cis type are present in natural foods & they are liquid at room temperature.
•They are classified according to the number of double bonds in their chains into two main groups:
▪Monoenoic acids: Contain one double bond.
▪Polyenoic acids:
▸They have more than one double bond in their structure
▸Thus termed polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA).
▸They include two important families which are ω3 & ω6 PUFA.

•Sources:
▪Nuts, plant oils (Olive,sunflower,cottonseed,corn, flaxseed oils)
▪Fish oil are rich sources.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS › 3 According to the Existence of Double Bonds
sections.text:
•Intake of cis fatty acids may reduce incidence of atherosclerosis & cardiovascular disease
•They lower plasma cholesterol & triacylglycerol levels, lower blood pressure and decrease the tendency to intravascular thrombosis.
Trans Fatty acids:
•The two hydrogen atoms exist on opposite sides of the double bond.
•Trans fatty acids are solid at room temperature.
•Sources:
▪Very small amounts of trans-unsaturated fatty acids are found in butter
▪The main source in human diet is from partially hydrogenated vegetable oils ( margarine).
▪They are present in many commercial baked foods like cakes and cookies, frozen pizza and most fried foods.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS › 3 According to the Existence of Double Bonds
sections.text:
•Trans FAs compete with essential fatty acids & may exacerbate essential FA deficiency.
•Also, they are structurally similar to saturated fatty acids, thus they can worsen hypercholesterolemia & atherosclerosis.

sections.heading:
4 NutritionalClassification
02 FATTY ACIDS › B CLASSIFICATION OF FATTY ACIDS
sections.text:
A. Essential Fatty Acids:
•They are not synthesized in our body, so it is essential to take them in diet.
•They include α-linolenic and linoleic acids.
•Arachidonic acid is synthesized in our bodies from linoleic acid, but in the absence of linoleic acid, it will be considered as an essential fatty acid.
•Importance of essential fatty acids:
▪Formation of healthy cell membrane.
▪Provide arachidonic acid for synthesis of eicosanoids (discussed later).
B. Non-Essential Fatty Acids:
•They include all other fatty acids because they are formed in our body in good amounts mainly from carbohydrates.
•It is not essential to take them in diet.

03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS
sections.text:
•Lipids are classified into three main groups according to their composition:
▪Simple lipids: Esters of fatty acids with various alcohols.
▪Compound (Conjugated) lipids: In addition to esters of fatty acids with alcohol, another group is added.
▪Derived lipids: They are fat soluble products of hydrolysis of the first two groups, or present in association with them in nature.

sections.heading:
A SIMPLE LIPIDS
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS
sections.text:
•They are esters of fatty acids with alcohol.
•According to the types of alcohol, there are two main subgroups:
▪Neutral fats (Triacylglycerol TAG): They are esters of three fatty acids with glycerol.
▪Waxes: They are esters of one fatty acid with long chain monohydroxy alcohol higher than glycerol.
•Triacylglycerol (Triglyceride):
▪Glycerol alcohol is liquid and soluble in water.
▪The fatty acids present in TAG are usually of different types (mixed TAG).
•Triglycerides are classified into:
▪Oils: They are liquid at room temperature due to their high content of USFA.
▪Solid fats: They are solid at room temperature due to their high content of long chains SFA.

sections.heading:
B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS
sections.text:
•They contain fatty acids, alcohol, and other groups.
•According to the type of the attached group, They are classified into:
▪Phospholipids: Containing phosphate group.
▪Glycolipids: Containing carbohydrate group.

•They are classified according to the alcohol present into two main sub-groups:
▪Glycerophospholipids: Containing glycerol.
▪Sphingomyelin: Containing sphingol.

sections.heading:
1 Glycerophospholipids
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS
sections.text:
•They are phospholipids containing glycerol.
•They include phosphatidic acid and its derivatives.
1Phosphatidic acid (Diacylglycerol phosphate):
•It is the parent compound of all other glycerophospholipids.
•On hydrolysis It gives:
▪One glycerol
▪One saturated FA (At position 1)
▪One unsaturated FA (At position 2)
▪Phosphoric acid (At position 3)
2Lecithin (Phosphatidylcholine):

•It is formed of phosphatidic acid and choline.
3Cephalin (Phosphatidylethanolamine):
•Formed of phosphatidic acid and ethanolamine.
4Phosphatidylinositol:
•Formed of phosphatidic acid and inositol.
5Plasmalogens:
•They resemble lecithin and cephalin but contain fatty alcohol instead of fatty acid at position 1 of their phosphatidic acids.

sections.heading:
Common Functions of Phospholipids
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS › 1 Glycerophospholipids
sections.text:
•Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules that contain non-polar groups of fatty acid side chains and polar groups of glycerol, phosphate, serine, ethanolamine, choline & inositol.
•Being amphipathic molecules:
1They are good emulsifying factors, that fractionate large fat globules into fine droplets with larger surface area. This is particularly important in digestion and absorption of dietary fats.
2They are good hydrotropic substances, they prevent deposition of cholesterol as cholesterol stones (biliary calculi).
3They are important constituents of plasma lipoproteins.
•They provide arachidonic acid and other PUFAs for synthesis of eicosanoids.
•They are important constituents of lipid bilayer of cell membranes.

sections.heading:
Note !!
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS › 1 Glycerophospholipids
sections.text: •Increased unsaturated fatty acids (USFA) content (at C2 of phospholipids) will increase membrane fluidity, because the kinks of the cis-double bonds prevent the packing of phospholipids closely together.

sections.heading:
Special Functions of some important Glycerophospholipids
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS › 1 Glycerophospholipids
sections.text:
1. Cephalin:
▪Increases thrombin formation, thus essential for blood clotting.
2. Phosphatidylinositol:
▪Acts as second messenger to many chemical transmitters, hormones and growth factors.
3. Lecithin:
•It provides choline for synthesis of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
•Lecithin is important as lung surfactant:
▪Lung surfactant is a naturally secreted material by pneumocytes and is formed mainly of dipalmitoyl-lecithin.
▪It reduces the tension between air of the alveoli and the alveolar membrane to facilitate trans-membrane passage of O2/CO2.
▪Otherwise, the alveolar membrane collapses resulting in respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) which is particularly developed in premature infants.
▪Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio (L/S ratio) is a marker of fetal lung maturity.
4. Plasmalogens:
•They provide the platelet activating factor (PAF) that enhances platelet aggregation, thus essential for blood clotting.
•They are abundant in the muscles and the nervous system, and their reduced levels have been associated with Alzheimer disease.

sections.heading:
Hydrolysis of glycerophospholipids
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS › 1 Glycerophospholipids
sections.text:
•They are hydrolyzed by a group of enzymes called phospholipases (PLA1, PLA2, PLC and PLD).
•Phospholipase D is not present in humans but present only in plants.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS › 1 Glycerophospholipids
sections.text:
•Snake venom toxins contain lecithinase enzyme with PLA2activity
•When injected into blood, it converts phospholipids present in cell membranes of RBCs into lysophospholipids causing cell membrane rupture (Hemolysis).
•Therefore, snake venom toxins cause death if not treated with antitoxins

sections.heading:
2 Sphingomyelin
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › B COMPOUND (CONJUGATED) LIPIDS
sections.text:
•Formed of sphingol (18C amino alcohol) attached to fatty acid and phosphocholine.
•Site: cell membranes of the lungs and brain (mainly in the myelin sheath).

•They are formed of sphingol, fatty acid and carbohydrate radical (s).
•As cerebrosides which are formed of sphingol, FA, and glucose or galactose.
•Importance of glycolipids:
▪They are found mainly in brain tissues, myelin sheath and cell membrane of RBCs.
▪They are components of cell membrane receptors for hormones and other ligands

sections.heading:
C DRIVED LIPID
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS
sections.text:
•They are products of hydrolysis of either simple or conjugated lipids or associated with lipids in nature.
•They include the following:
1Fatty acids
2Alcohols
3Steroids
4Fat soluble vitamins: vitamins A, D, E & K (discussed later)
5Carotenoids: (Discussed later).

•They are compounds containing steroid nucleus.
•It is composed of 4 fused rings with 17 carbon atoms.
•Classification of steroids:
▪They include the following groups:
1Sterols
2Bile acids
3Steroid hormones

sections.heading:
1 Sterols
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › C DRIVED LIPID
sections.text:
•Sterols mean solid alcohol.
•Cholesterol is the most important sterol in animals.

sections.heading:
CHOLESTEROL
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › C DRIVED LIPID › 1 Sterols
sections.text:
•Sources:
▪Exogenous (Dietary):
▸The richest sources are egg yolk, meat, liver, kidney, butter, and brain.
▸It is the most important animal sterol.
▪Endogenous:
▸Every cell, apart from RBCs, can synthesize its own cholesterol (from acetyl CoA).
▸Plasma cholesterol is synthesized by the liver and intestine.
•Forms:
▪It is present either free (non-esterified) or esterified with fatty acid to form cholesteryl-ester. Free cholesterol contains 27 carbon atoms.
•Plasma level of cholesterol:
▪Normally it ranges from 120 to 200 mg/dL (Recommended level is < 200 mg/dL).
▪About 30% as free cholesterol and 70% as cholesteryl-esters.
•Importance and derivatives of cholesterol:
▪It is an important constituent of cell membranes that controls their fluidity.
▪It is the precursor of all steroid hormones.
▪It is converted to vitamin D3under the skin by ultraviolet rays.
▪It is converted into bile acids and bile salts in the liver.

sections.heading:
2 Steroid Hormones
03 CLASSIFICATION OF LIPIDS › C DRIVED LIPID
sections.text:
•Sex hormones:
▪Male sex hormones: e.g., testosterone (C19)
▪Female sex hormones: e.g., estrogen (C18) and progesterone (C21)
•Corticoids: (C21)
▪Glucocorticoids: e.g., cortisol
▪Mineralocorticoids: e.g., aldosterone

sections.text:
•Eicosanoids are physiologically active compounds formed from polyunsaturated FAs with C20 e.g., arachidonic acid.
•Arachidonic acid is liberated from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2or synthesized from the ω-6 essential fatty acid linoleate.

sections.heading:
A CLASSIFICATION
04 EICOSANOIDS
sections.text:
•Eicosanoids are classified into two main groups:
▪Cyclic compounds:
▸[Prostaglandins (PG), prostacyclins (PGI) and thromboxanes (TX)]
▸These are formed from C20 PUFA
▸Examples: Arachidonic acid, by action of the enzyme prostaglandin H synthase.
▸This enzyme has two catalytic activities: cyclooxygenase (COX) and peroxidase.
▪Acyclic compounds:
▸[Leukotrienes (LT) and lipoxins (LX)]
▸Formed from C20 PUFA (e.g., arachidonic acid) by action of lipoxygenase.

sections.heading:
B EFFECTS OF SOME EICOSANOIDS
04 EICOSANOIDS

Biomedical Correlation
04 EICOSANOIDS › B EFFECTS OF SOME EICOSANOIDS
sections.text:
•Steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (SAID):
▪They inhibit phospholipase A2activity. Thus, decrease availability of arachidonic acid.
▪For example: hydrocortisone (cortisol).
•Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID):
▪They inhibit cyclooxygenase activity. Thus, inhibit PG synthesis.
▪They include Aspirin and other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen).
▪Aspirin produces acetylation of the hydroxyl group of serine at the active site of cyclooxygenase enzyme, explaining the anti-inflammatory and antipyretic actions of aspirin.
•Singulair:
▪It is leukotriene receptor antagonist.
▪It relieves bronchospasm and inhibits allergic pathway (used to treat severe bronchial asthmatic attacks and allergies).

02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES
sections.text:
•Each nucleoside is formed of a nitrogenous base and a pentose (Ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA), where C1` of the pentose forms N-linked glycosidic bond with N1 of a pyrimidine or N9 of a purine.
•Each nucleotide is formed of a nitrogenous base, pentose, and phosphate
•The phosphate group is usually attached by ester bond to the terminal alcohol group of the pentose (Termed 5`hydroxyl group).

sections.heading:

sections.text: •Nucleosides and nucleotides are named according to their nitrogenous bases

sections.heading:
2 EnergyTransduction
02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES › C BIOLOGICALIMPORTANCE
sections.text:
•Examples:
▪Adenosine mono,di and triphosphate (AMP, ADP, ATP)
▪Guanosine mono,di and triphosphate (GMP, GDP, GTP)
•ATP is used as a source of energy in all mechanical or chemical processes muscular exercise, nerve impulse, cell membrane transport, anabolic reactions, and phosphorylation of compounds).
•When there is a need for energy, ATP is converted to ADP or AMP.
•The bonds between α-β and β-γ phosphate groups are high energy bonds (~)

•GTP is also an energy source in some metabolic processes.

sections.heading:
3 Signaling Second Messengers
02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES › C BIOLOGICALIMPORTANCE
sections.text:
•Examples:
▪Cyclic 3`,5` Adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
▪Cyclic 3`,5` Guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)

sections.heading:
cAMP
02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES › C BIOLOGICALIMPORTANCE › 3 Signaling Second Messengers
sections.text:
•It’s is formed from ATP by adenylyl cyclase & it is converted to AMP by phosphodiesterase.
•Hormone-receptor interaction produces activation of G proteins, which produce activation of adenylyl cyclase, the latter forms cAMP from ATP.
•Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A → Causes phosphorylationof proteins (e.g enzymes).
•Conversion of dephosphorylated enzyme to phosphorylated enzyme causes either its activation e.g., glycogen phosphorylase kinase or its inactivation e.g., glycogen synthase.
•Inactive protein kinase is a tetramer formed of 2 regulatory (R) & 2 catalytic subunits (C).
•Binding of 2 molecules of cAMP to each of regulatory subunits causes release of 2 catalytic subunits, which are active and catalyze phosphorylation of its substrate (s) i.e., conversion of dephosphorylated enzyme(s) into phosphorylated enzyme(s).
•This process is reversed by a protein phosphatase → Produces enzyme dephosphorylation
•Many hormones act through this mechanism e.g. glucagon and epinephrine activate adenylyl cyclase and increase cAMP which in turn inhibits protein phosphatase.
•While Insulin activates protein phosphatase and phosphodiesterase enzymes and decreases cAMP level (i.e. reverses the effects of glucagon and epinephrine).

sections.heading:
cGMP
02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES › C BIOLOGICALIMPORTANCE › 3 Signaling Second Messengers
sections.text:
•It is formed from GTP by guanylyl cyclase.
•It acts as a second messenger.
•Many vasodilators cause smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation by activating guanylyl cyclase and increasing cGMP e.g., nitric oxide

sections.text:
A. S-Adenosyl methionine (Active Methionine) or (SAM)
•Active methionine is a nucleoside and is formed in body from methionine&ATP.

•It is used for synthesis of sulfur containing compounds in the body

C. Cytidine diphosphate choline (CDP-choline) ,CDP-ethanolamine or CDP-diacylglycerol

•R is choline, ethanolamine or diacylglycerol,They are used for phospholipid synthesis.
D. Uridine diphosphate (UDP)

•R is glucose, galactose, or glucuronic acid.
▪UDP-Glc is used for synthesis of glycogen, glycoproteins, andglycolipids.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
02 NUCLEOSIDES AND NUCLEOTIDES › C BIOLOGICALIMPORTANCE › 5 Coenzymes Components
sections.text:
•Synthetic base analogs
▪They are chemical compounds that are structurally similar to naturally occurring purines and pyrimidines.
▪They can be incorporated into DNA or RNA during replication or transcription, so they are powerful tool in medicine and molecular biology.
▪They are used as anti-cancer or anti-viral agents.
▸Anti-cancer drugs: 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) inhibits purine & nucleic acid synthesis.
▸Antiviral Drugs: Acycloguanosine (Acyclovir) → Inhibits viral DNA synthesis only with no effect on host cells .

sections.heading:
A DIETARY PURINES AND PYRIMIDINES
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES
sections.text:
•They are mainly present in the form of nucleic acids.
•Nucleic acids are found mostly in the liver and meat.
•Little amounts are present in legumes, cereals, and vegetables.

sections.heading:
B DIGESTION
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES

C FATE
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES
sections.text:
•Absorbed purines are oxidized (In the liver) to uric acid which is excreted in urine.
•Absorbed pyrimidines are catabolized (In the liver) to CO2, NH3, and β-amino acids.
•Little or no dietary purines or pyrimidines are incorporated into the body’s nucleic acids
•Therefore, nucleic acids and nucleotides obtained from the diet are not considered essential, as the human body can synthesize them endogenously.

sections.heading:
BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES

A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
sections.text:
•In de novo synthesis, the purine ring is synthesized stepwise from simple precursor molecules on a ribose phosphate backbone to form inosine monophosphate (IMP), the precursor of AMP and GMP.

•Main Steps of De Novo Synthesis:

sections.heading:
1 Synthesis of -5phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP)
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•PRPP is the activated form of ribose phosphate and is an essential precursor in purine and pyrimidine synthesis.
•It is synthesized from ribose-5-phosphate, which is produced through the hexose monophosphate pathway (Pathway of glucose oxidation).
•This reaction is catalyzed by PRPP synthetase enzyme.

sections.heading:
2 Synthesis of phosphoribosylamine
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•N9of the purine ring is provided by the amide group of glutamine forming 5-phosphoribosylamine.
•This reaction is catalyzed by an enzyme termed glutamine: PRPP amidotransferase.
•This is the key step in de novo purine nucleotide synthesis.

sections.heading:
3 Synthesis of Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS
sections.text: •It is formed by the addition of different atoms to the NH2group of phosphoribosylamine using specific intermediates or precursors till the first purine is formed by ring closure which is inosine-monophosphate (IMP).

sections.heading:
Note !!
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS › 3 Synthesis of Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
sections.text:
•Folic acid is important in the biosynthesis of purines (C-2 and C-8).
•Thus, folate antagonists (e.g., methotrexate) inhibit purine and nucleic acid synthesis, leading to inhibition of cell division, and hence their use in the treatment of some cancers.

sections.heading:
4 Conversion of IMP AMP and GMP
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › A DE NOVO SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•IMP acts as a precursor of other purine nucleotides:
▪IMP → XMP → GMP
▪IMP → Adenylosuccinate → AMP

6 Synthesis of Deoxyribonucleotides

sections.text:
•This is catalyzed by an enzyme complex termed ribonucleotide reductase
•which is active only during DNA synthesis and inhibited mainly by dATP.

sections.heading:
B PURINE SALVAGE SYSTEM
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
sections.text:
•The significance of the purine salvage system is to supply purine nucleotides to tissues where the de novo synthesis is not active e.g., brain and precursors of red blood cells.
•There are 2 systems for purine salvage:

sections.heading:
1 Salvage of free purines
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › B PURINE SALVAGE SYSTEM

2 Salvage of purine nucleosides
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › B PURINE SALVAGE SYSTEM

1 Feedback regulation
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › C REGULATION OF BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
sections.text:
•De novo purine nucleotide synthesis is a good example for multiple loops feedback inhibition.
•High concentration of IMP, AMP, ADP, GMP and GDP produce feedback inhibition of conversion of ribose-5-phosphate to IMP at two sites:
▪PRPP synthetase
▪Glutamine:PRPP- amidotransferase.

sections.heading:
2 Availability of the substrates
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES › C REGULATION OF BIOSYNTHESIS OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
sections.text: •The rate of the reaction catalyzed by glutamine: PRPP-amidotransferase is controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP and glutamine.

sections.heading:
CATABOLISM OF PURINE NUCLEOTIDES
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES
sections.text:
•Purine nucleotides are degraded through a series of enzymatic reactions to form uric acid
•Uric acid the end product of purine catabolism in humans.
•Uric acid is the main end product of purine catabolism in the human liver.
•Plasma uric acid (Urate) levels are 4-7 mg/dL for males & 3-6 mg/dL for females during fasting.
•Excretion of Uric acid:
▪In normal adult humans, the daily excretion of uric acid is about 400-600 mg.
▪Urate salts are more soluble than uric acid.
▪So, the pH of urine influences the solubility of uric acid e.g., urine at pH 5 can dissolve only about one-tenth as much as urine at pH 7.
•Therefore, alkalization of urine markedly increases solubility of uric acid & promotes its excretion.

sections.heading:
I. Hyperuricemia
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES
sections.text: •Hyperuricemia or elevated serum urate levels results from over production (metabolic) or decreased excretion (Renal).

sections.heading:
1 Increased Production of uric acid
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › I. Hyperuricemia › A CAUSES OF GOUT
sections.text:
1. Dietary causes:
•Excess intake of nucleoprotein rich diet (cellular proteins) e.g., meat, liver & kidney.
2. Metabolic Gout:
•Primary Metabolic Gout: This is due to genetic disorders as follows:
▪Defects of PRPP synthetase: Due to genetic mutation, the enzyme is either superactive or resistant to feedback inhibition.
▪Partial deficiency of HGPRTase of purine salvage system.
▪Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome: Complete deficiency of HGPRTase.
▪Von Gierke’s disease (Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency) due to enhanced synthesis & degradation of purine & decreased excretion of uric acid
•Secondary Metabolic Gout: It is due to diseases which cause increase in purine catabolism e.g., cancer, leukemia, and psoriasis.

sections.heading:
2 Decreased Excretion of uric acid (Renal Gout)
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › I. Hyperuricemia › A CAUSES OF GOUT
sections.text:
•Primary Renal Gout: It is due to primary or congenital renal disease.
•Secondary Renal Gout: It is due to acquired renal disease.
•Alcohol intake:
▪Alcohol metabolism increases lactate production, resulting in lactic acidosis.
▪Lactate competes with uric acid for renal tubular secretion.
▪Because lactate is present in higher concentration, it reduces uric acid excretion leading to hyperuricemia and gout.
▪In addition, alcohol intake causes dehydration → Decreases uric acid excretion.

sections.heading:
1 Diet
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › I. Hyperuricemia › B TREATMENT OF GOUT
sections.text:
•Restriction of nucleoprotein rich diet (Cellular proteins) e.g., meat, liver and kidney, the best are non-cellular proteins as milk and its products.
•Maintaining adequate fluid intake helps to decrease the risk of kidney stone formation.
•Avoid alcohol intake.

sections.heading:
2 Drugs
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES › I. Hyperuricemia › B TREATMENT OF GOUT
sections.text:
1. Anti-inflammatory agents:
•They are used to decrease joint inflammation and to relief pain.
2. Drugs decreasing the production of uric acid:
•Allopurinol is the drug of choice:
▪It competitively inhibits xanthine oxidase as it has a structural similarity to hypoxanthine (see competitive enzyme inhibitors).
▪Allopurinol is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to oxypurinol.
▪The latter binds tightly to xanthine oxidase, inhibiting its ability to oxidize hypoxanthine and xanthine and decreases uric acid formation.
▪Also, the reaction of allopurinol with PRPP results in a decrease in PRPP levels and thus decreases de novo purine synthesis.

sections.heading:
II. Hypouricemia
03 METABOLISM OF PURINES & PYRIMIDINES
sections.text:
•It is caused mainly by adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
•The high levels of dATP inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, which inhibits DNA synthesis.
•Therefore, white blood cells can’t proliferate resulting in impairment of T-cell & B-cell functions.

•The main end products of pyrimidine catabolism are CO2, NH3, β-alanine (uracil& cytosine) or β-aminoisobutyrate (thymine) which are highly water soluble and easily excreted.

sections.heading: IN THIS CHAPTER — The molecular language of genetic information
sections.text:
01 Introduction to Nucleic Acids
02 Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA)

sections.heading: 01 INTRODUCTION TO NUCLEIC ACIDS AND GENETIC STRUCTURE
sections.text:
•Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides.
•There are 2 main types of nucleic acids: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) & Ribonucleic acid (RNA).
•Responsible mainly for storage & transfer of information needed for production of proteins.

sections.heading: 02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA)
sections.text:
•It consists of two strands of polynucleotides
•It has the following primary, secondary, and tertiary structures:

sections.heading:
A DNA PRIMARY STRUCTURE
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA)
sections.text:
•The nucleotides that form DNA primary structure are mainly 4:
▪dAMP,dGMP,dCMP& dTMP.
•In each strand, nucleotides are linked together by phosphodiester bonds between:
▪The 3`-hydroxyl group of the pentose sugar of one nucleotide
▪The 5`-hydroxyl group of the pentose sugar of the next nucleotide
▪Joind through a phosphate group.
•This forms an alternating sugar phosphate backbone of each DNA strand (5`-P-S-P-S3-`).
•The nitrogenous bases, which are linked to the pentoses, are projecting to the inside of the two strands of DNA at right angles.
•The sequence of bases determines the coding structure of DNA (Genetic information).
•Each polynucleotide strand has two terminals.
•One end has a free phosphate group attached to the 5`-hydroxyl group of the first pentose and the other end has a free 3`- hydroxyl group of the terminal pentose.
•The order of nucleotides in any DNA strand is always written in the 5` to 3`direction which is the direction of synthesis, e.g., AGCT in the figure below.

sections.heading:
B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA)
sections.text:
•Watson and Crick proposed a structure for DNA in the form of a double helix.
•It has the following characteristics:

sections.heading:
1 Two antiparallel strands form a right-handed double helix
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
sections.text: •The two strands of DNA run antiparallel and are paired to each other and coil around a common axis to form a right-handed helix (see figure).

sections.heading:
2 Complementary base pairing
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
sections.text:
•The two strands are held together by complementary base pairing through specific hydrogen bonds.
•Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

sections.heading:
3 Base stacking
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
sections.text:
•The base pairs inside the helix are stacked above each other by Van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions.
•These forces provide thestability of the double helix.

sections.heading:
4 Spiral staircase
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
sections.text: •The double helix of DNA appears much like spiral staircase, in which base pairs form the steps and the phosphate sugar backbones form thehandrails.

sections.heading:
5 Dimensions
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA)
sections.text:
•The DNA is 2 nm in width.
•From outside of helix, 2 grooves are apparent, a major groove (2.2 nm in length) and a minor groove (1.2nm in length).
•Through these grooves many drugs and proteins can contact the nitrogenous bases without any need to open the helix.

sections.heading:
Denaturation of DNA
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › B DNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE, DOUBLE HELIX (dsDNA) › 5 Dimensions
sections.text:
•Heating DNA produces rupture of hydrogen bondsand separation of the two strands of DNA or DNA denaturation.
•Cooling of denatured DNA results in reformation of the double helix or renaturation or reannealing
•Denaturation of DNA is the first step in the in-vitro amplification technique “Polymerase Reaction (PCR)”.

sections.heading:
C DNA TERTIARY STRUCTURES
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA)
sections.text:
•The length of human DNA per cell is approximately 2 meters, and the diameter of the nucleus is 10 microns.
•Supercoiling of DNA is important for its packing within the small nucleus.
•Each DNA molecule is condensed into a compact structure about 10 μm long and 1 μm in diameter through differentlevels of supercoiling

special proteins.
•The protein/DNA complex is called chromatin
•Each chromatid contains:

sections.heading:
2 Histone proteins
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › C DNA TERTIARY STRUCTURES
sections.text:
•They are basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine (Positively charged), that are united to DNA which is acidic (Negatively charged due to the presence of phosphate groups).
•Five major types of histones (H1, H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) are present in eukaryotic chromosomes.
•They interact with the minor grooves of DNA.
•The main function of the histone proteins is to condense the DNA intostructural units called “Nucleosomes”.
•Each nucleosome is formed of eight histones (Histone octamer or histone core), i.e., two copies of each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
•Around the histone octamer, one and three quarters of supercoiled DNA segment is wrapped (Contains an average of 140 bp).
•Linker or spacer DNA (Contains an average of 60 bp) connects different nucleosomes.
•H1 is attached to linker DNA.
•Connection of nucleosomes by linker DNA makes chromatin looks like beads on a string.
•Nucleosomes are further arranged into more complex structures that organize and condense the long DNA molecule into chromatids.

sections.heading:
3 Non-histone proteins
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › C DNA TERTIARY STRUCTURES
sections.text:
•They interact with the major grooves.
•They share in the packing of DNA and are important for regulation of gene expression and involved in replication and transcription.

sections.heading:
Mitochondrial DNA (mt-DNA)
02 DEOXYRIBONUCLEIC ACID (DNA) › C DNA TERTIARY STRUCTURES › 3 Non-histone proteins
sections.text:
•DNA is mainly linear but sometimes it is circular as in DNA of mitochondria,chloroplasts (In plants) and bacteria.
•Mitochondrial DNA represents 0.3 to 1% of the total cellular DNA.
•Human mt-DNA is present in the form of a small double stranded circular supercoil.
•It is responsible for controlling synthesis of 2 rRNA, 22 tRNA and 13 proteins, most of these mitochondrial proteins are involved in oxidative phosphorylation (Electron transport chain and ATP synthesis).
•Mitochondria are provided by the ovum, thus mt-DNA molecules are maternally inherited and are used as maternal lineage.
•Mutations of mt-DNA are associated with certain types of myopathies.

sections.heading: 03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA)
sections.text:
•There are three major types of RNAs that participate in the process of protein synthesis:
▪Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
▪Transfer RNA (tRNA)
▪Messenger RNA (mRNA)

sections.heading:
A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA)
sections.text:
•RNAs represent about 15% of the total RNA in the cell.
•Each tRNA serves as a carrier to its specific amino acid during translation.
•There is at least one specific type of tRNA molecule for each of the twenty amino acids commonly found in proteins.
•tRNA molecule is a single strand folded to form a cloverleaf appearancestabilized by hydrogen bonds.
•tRNA molecule has 4 main arms and one extra arm:

sections.heading:
1 The acceptor arm
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
sections.text:
•It terminates at its 3` OH end by a specific sequence formed of CCA.
•Amino acids are carried in the form of aminoacyl group connected to the 3`-hydroxyl group of the acceptor arm.

sections.heading:
2 D-arm
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
sections.text:
•Contains an unusual base dihydrouracil.
•D-arm is important for recognition of tRNA by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme which catalyzes the binding of a specific amino acid to its specific tRNA

sections.heading:
3 Anticodon arm
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
sections.text:
•Contains 3 specific bases known as anticodon.
•This portion of tRNA plays a key role in translation

by pairing with complementary codon of mRNA.

sections.heading:
4 Ψ
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
sections.text:
•Contains the unusual specific sequence of thymine and pseudouridine bases.
•This arm is important for binding tRNA to ribosome during the process of protein synthesis.

sections.heading:
5 Extra arm
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › A TRANSFER RNAs(tRNAs)
sections.text: •Contains from 3 to 12 bases (with no base pairing) & the major site for variation in tRNA

sections.heading:
B MESSENGER RNAs (mRNAs)
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA)
sections.text:
•Messenger RNAs represent only about 5% of the RNA in the cell.
•The coding region of mRNA carries genetic information from nuclear DNA to the cytosol, where it is used as the template for protein synthesis (Each 3 bases or codon, designate an amino acid).
•The coding region of mRNA starts with a specific initiation codon and ends with a specific termination codon.
•Untranslated regions (UTRs) are sections of the mRNA before the initiationcodon and after the termination codon that are not translated, termed the five prime untranslated regions (5’ UTRs) and the three prime untranslated regions (3’ UTRs), respectively.
•These regions are transcribed with coding region & they are present in the mature mRNA.
•Several functionsin gene expression have been attributed to the untranslated regions, including mRNA stability, translational efficiency and regulation of gene expression.

sections.heading:
C RIBOSOMAL RNAs (rRNAs)
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA)
sections.text:
•The rRNAs represent about 80% of the total RNA of the cell.
•They are found in association with several proteins as components of theribosomes and serve as the sites for protein synthesis.
•The fully active 80S ribosomes are formed mainly of two main nucleoprotein subunits of unequal size, the 60S subunit and the 40S subunit.
•The Svedberg unit (Sedimentation or Sunit) is a measure of the sedimentation velocity by high-speed centrifuge, which depends on the molecular weight as well as the size of the particles i.e., particle density.

sections.heading:
D OTHER FORMS OF RNAs (NON-CODING RNAs)
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA)
sections.text: •Required for regulation of transcription & translation

sections.heading:
1 Nuclear non-coding RNAs
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › D OTHER FORMS OF RNAs (NON-CODING RNAs)
sections.text:
•Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs):
▪Involved in mRNA processing as components of spliceosomes (See transcription)
•Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs):
▪They modify rRNAs to ensure proper ribosome assembly during protein synthesis

sections.heading:
2 Regulatory non-coding RNAs
03 RIBONUCLEIC ACID (RNA) › D OTHER FORMS OF RNAs (NON-CODING RNAs)
sections.text:
•Including many types, some of which are:
▪MicroRNAs (miRNAs):
▸They have important role in regulating gene expression by many mechanisms, mainly by targeting mRNA molecules and degrading them.
▪Circular RNA (circRNA):
▸They are present in the form of closed loop molecules that act as miRNA sponges (i.e. they bind to miRNAs, preventing them from targeting mRNA, thus acting as inhibitors).
▪long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs):
▸Important in epigenetic regulationgene expression (See later).

sections.heading:
A GENES
04 GENETIC TERMINOLOGY
sections.text:
•A gene is an element of heredity, transmitted from parents to offspring in reproduction.
•Chemically, a gene is a sequence of nucleotides along a DNA molecule.
•Most eukaryotic genes are discontinuous i.e., coding sequences (Exons) separated by noncoding sequences (Introns).
•Coding sequences are unique & non-repetitive while noncoding sequences are repetitive.

sections.heading:
B CHROMOSOME
04 GENETIC TERMINOLOGY
sections.text:
•A thread-like structure of DNA and proteins found in the nucleus of most living cells
•Carry genetic information in the form of genes
•Divides longitudinally during cell division into two chromatids.

sections.heading:
C GENOME
04 GENETIC TERMINOLOGY
sections.text: •It is the total genetic information presented by the group of chromosomes in any cell.

sections.heading:
D GENOTYPE
04 GENETIC TERMINOLOGY
sections.text: •If the two genes (Alleles) in an individual are similar, the genotype is homozygous for these genes, if 2 genes are different from each other, the genotype is said to be heterozygous.

sections.heading:
E PHENOTYPE
04 GENETIC TERMINOLOGY
sections.text: •It is the outside or the observable traits depending on the genotype of the individual.

sections.heading: 01 INTRODUCTION TO DNA REPLICATION
sections.text:
•Central dogma of molecular biology:
▪It is the process in which genetic information flows from DNA to RNA, to make a functional product protein.
•DNA replication is the process by which a double strand DNA molecule is copied to produce two identical daughter DNA molecules catalyzed mainly by DNA polymerases.

•Each parental strand of the DNA molecule acts as a template for the formation of a complementary new DNA strand.
•Therefore, each of the daughter DNA molecules is composed of one original (conserved) strand and one newly synthesized strand → This is called semi-conservative replication.
•The major function of replication is “Genetic continuity”, i.e. ensuring that daughter cells receive identical genetic material during cell division.

sections.heading:
1 Opening of DNA at multiple Origins of replication
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › A SEPARATION OF THE TWO DNA STRANDS:
sections.text:
•Many origins across the chromosomes (rich in AT base pairs) serve as starting points for replication.
•They are recognized by origin recognition complex (ORC) proteins.
•ORC proteins bind to the replication origins & produce local opening & unwinding of DNA double helix.
•Presence of multiple replication origins markedly decreases time needed for replication.

sections.heading:
2 Formation of Two Replication Forks in each replication origin
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › A SEPARATION OF THE TWO DNA STRANDS:
sections.text:
•Helicase enzyme molecules are attached to each origin and unwind the DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous base pairs forming “Replication bubbles”.
•Single strand binding (SSB) proteins:
▪They bind to the single strands of unwound parts of DNA & stabilize the single strands.
▪In the absence of SSB proteins, the two strands can rewind again.
▪Also, they protect single strand from nucleases that cleave single strand DNA.
•By the action of helicase and SSB proteins, a replication fork is created.

sections.heading:
B INITIATION OF DNA SYNTHESIS: FORMATION OF RNA PRIMERS
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION
sections.text:
•At the replication fork, both strands of parental DNA serve as templates for DNA synthesis.
•DNA polymerases cannot initiate DNA synthesis without the presence of RNA primers.
•RNA primers are short segments of RNA used as a binding sites for DNA polymerase.
•They are formed by the action of:
▪DNA polymerase α-primase complex & base-paired to the parental strand.
•The 5`- end of the primer is attached to the 3’- end of the parental strand, and the 3`- end of the primer will accept the first deoxynucleotide.

sections.heading:
C ELONGATION (SYNTHESIS OF DNA LEADING AND LAGGING STRANDS)
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION
sections.text:
•DNA polymerases are template-directed enzymes
•They are only able to read the parental nucleotide sequence in 3` to 5` direction
•Thus synthesize the new strands in 5` to 3` direction.
•DNA polymerases catalyze the formation of polynucleotide chains through the addition of free deoxy-ribonucleoside triphosphates & the removal of pyrophosphates forming phosphodiester bonds.
•Hydrogen bonds are then formed with complementary nucleotides on parental strands.

sections.heading:
1 Synthesis of the leading strand
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › C ELONGATION (SYNTHESIS OF DNA LEADING AND LAGGING STRANDS)
sections.text:
•DNA polymerase ε synthesizes the leading strand of DNA.
•Only one RNA primer is required by DNA polymerase ε.
•The leading strand is copied in the direction of the advancing replication fork.
•The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner in the 5` to 3` direction.

sections.heading:
2 Synthesis of the lagging strand
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › C ELONGATION (SYNTHESIS OF DNA LEADING AND LAGGING STRANDS)
sections.text:
•DNA-polymerase δ synthesizes the lagging strand of DNA.
•Multiple RNA primers are required by DNA polymerase δ.
•The lagging strand is copied in the opposite direction of the advancing replication fork.
•The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously in the form of short Okazaki fragments that are produced in a 5` to 3` direction.
•The length of these Okazaki fragments ranges from 100 to 200 bases.

sections.heading:
3 Proofreading of newly synthesized DNA strands
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › C ELONGATION (SYNTHESIS OF DNA LEADING AND LAGGING STRANDS)
sections.text:
•Misreading of the template sequence may result in permanent mutations.
•To avoid this, polymerases ε and δ have proof-reading activity.
•They remove the misplaced nucleotide (act as exonuclease) & replace it with the correct nucleotide.

sections.heading:
4 Removal of DNA supercoiling
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › C ELONGATION (SYNTHESIS OF DNA LEADING AND LAGGING STRANDS)
sections.text:
•When DNA unwinds, supercoils are formed during DNA replication.
•They are removed by DNA topoisomerases.

sections.heading:
1 Synthesis of the leading strand
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › D TERMINATION: REMOVAL OF PRIMERS AND JOINING OF FRAGMENTS
sections.text:
•RNase H removes the RNA primers by its exonuclease activity.
•DNA polymerase δ fills the gaps between Okazaki fragments.

sections.heading:
2 Joining of DNA fragments
02 STEPS OF EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION › D TERMINATION: REMOVAL OF PRIMERS AND JOINING OF FRAGMENTS
sections.text: •DNA ligase joins the ends of adjacent fragments using ATP.

sections.heading: 03 PRESERVATION OF CHROMOSOMAL ENDS BY TELOMERES
sections.text:
•The ends of the eukaryotic linear chromosomes are called telomeres.
•The 3`end strand of the telomere contains a non-coding region with specific sequence (5`-TTAGGG3-`) that is repeated thousands of times.
•The 3`end strand is longer than the complementary 5`end strand by a few hundred nucleotides.
•This part of the 3`end single strand is folded back on itself forming a loop like structure stabilized by protein.
•This loop structure prevents the stacking of chromosomes.
•Also, Protects the ends of chromosomes from being attacked & hydrolyzed by nuclease enzymes.

•During the process of replication, the leading strand can be synthesized to the end of the parent strand while the lagging strand cannot because:
▪Primase cannot act at the 3`end of the strand due to the narrow space.
▪If primase acts, the removal of the RNA primer would leave a short gap
▸As a result, telomeres shorten with each cell division.
▸If shortening continues → Affect important genes → Cells stop dividing & undergo aging.

sections.heading:
A ROLE OF TELOMERASE IN RESTORATION OF TELOMERES
03 PRESERVATION OF CHROMOSOMAL ENDS BY TELOMERES
sections.text:
•Telomerase is an enzyme with reverse transcriptase activity.
•A reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from RNA.
•Telomerase also contains a short internal RNA template complementary to the DNA sequence on 3` end strand of the telomere.
•Telomerase recognizes and binds to the single-strand 3` terminus.
•It elongates the 3`end by synthesizing DNA complementary to its internal RNA template.
•Telomerase repeats the process of elongation till the length of the 3` strand becomes suitable (about 100 nucleotides)
•It allows, Binding of a primer & the completion of synthesis of lagging DNA strand till end.

sections.heading:
B BIOMEDICAL APPLICATIONS OF TELOMERASE
03 PRESERVATION OF CHROMOSOMAL ENDS BY TELOMERES
04 SUMMARY OF ENZYMES REQUIRED FOR EUKARYOTIC REPLICATION
sections.text:
•DNA helicases: for unwinding and separation of the two DNA strands.
•DNA polymerases:
▪DNA polymerase α-primase complex: for synthesis of RNA primers & short DNA connected to the RNA primers.
▪DNA polymerase β: for DNA repair.
▪DNA polymerase γ: for mitochondrial DNA synthesis.
▪DNA polymerase δ: for synthesis of the lagging strand.
▪DNA polymerase ε: for synthesis of the leading strand.
•Topoisomerases: for removal of supercoils formed during DNA replication.
•RNase H: for removal of RNA primers.
•DNA ligase: to join the ends of adjacent DNA segments (ATP is required).
•Telomerase: for elongation of the 3`- end of telomeres of DNA.

sections.heading: 05 DNA REPAIR
sections.text:
•Replication process takes place at high accuracy, but an error can occur forevery 30,000bases.
•DNA is constantly subjected to environmental factors e.g., radiation and chemicals, that cause alteration or removal of nucleotide bases.
•Bases are also altered or lost spontaneously or during replication.
•If damage is not repaired, a permanent mutation occurs → May result in a hereditary disorder.
•The broad steps of repair are as follows:

sections.heading:
1 Recognition of the lesion:
05 DNA REPAIR
sections.text:
•This is the function of an endonuclease
•It cleaves damaged strand to form a cut (Nick).

sections.heading:
2 Excision of damaged DNA:
05 DNA REPAIR
sections.text: •The damaged part is removed by an exonuclease.

sections.heading:
3 Filling the gap:
05 DNA REPAIR
sections.text: •This is catalyzed by a repair DNA polymerase β.

sections.heading:
4 Ligation:
05 DNA REPAIR
sections.text: •This is catalyzed by DNA ligase.
