sections.heading: 01 INTRODUCTION TO GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text:
•Gene expression is the process by which the information contained within a gene becomes a functional product (RNA or protein).
•It generally happens in two main steps: Transcription and translation.

sections.heading: 02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION)
sections.text: Synthesis of RNA from DNA is known as transcription.

sections.heading:
A PRINCIPLES OF TRANSCRIPTION AND TERMINOLOGY
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION)
sections.text:
•Only one strand of DNA is transcribed.
•The strand of DNA that is transcribed into RNA is known as the template strand whereas the other strand is known as the coding strand.
•The sequence of RNA is complementary to the sequence of template strand, and it is the same as that of coding strand except for U replacing T.
•RNA synthesis includes four main phases: Preinitiation, Initiation, Elongation & Termination.

•Start site: The first nucleotide at the 3’ end of the transcription region of the template strand is designated as +1.
•Upstream: The 3’ direction of the template strand before the start site (+1) takes negative numbers -1 ,-2 ,-3 …. etc.
•Downstream: The5’direction of the template strand afterthestartsite(+1) takes positive numbers
•Promoter: The nucleotide sequence in the template strand at which the RNA polymerase begins attachment. It lies upstream the transcription region and marks the beginning.
•Terminator: The nucleotide sequence in the template strand lies downstream the transcription region and marks the end.
•Transcription region: The nucleotide sequence transcribed by RNA polymerase.
•Transcription unit: It includes the promoter, the transcription region, and the terminator.

•The basic mechanism of RNA synthesis is the same for all types of RNAs:
▪Messenger (mRNAs), ribosomal (rRNAs) and transfer (tRNAs).
•The synthesis of RNA is catalysed by a group of enzymes termed RNA polymerases.

sections.heading:
A TYPES OF RNA POLYMERASES
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION)
sections.text:
•There are three types of nuclear RNA polymerases:
▪RNA polymerase I and III: For synthesis of rRNAs and tRNAs mainly.
▪RNA polymerase II: For synthesis of mRNAs, most small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) and micro RNAs (miRNAs).

sections.heading:
RNA
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION)
sections.text:
m
•RNA polymerase II is responsible for synthesis of mRNAs.
•The promoter : Two types of sequence elements are present in eukaryotic promoter and are called the “Basal expression elements”.

sections.heading:
1 TATA box:
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › RNA
sections.text:
•It defines where transcription is to start along the DNA.
•It has the sequence of TATAAA.
•It is usually located (-20-30 bp) upstream of the transcription start site.

sections.heading:
2 CAAT box and GC box:
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › RNA
sections.text:
•They define when transcription is to start
•They control how frequently this event occurs
•They are located (-40-200 bp) upstream of the transcription start site.

sections.heading:
1 Pre-initiation
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › C STEPS OF TRANSCRIPTION
sections.text:
•Transcriptional factors involved in this step are TFII A, B, D, E, F and H
•TFIID binds to the TATA box promoter element.
•It is the only one of these factors that is independently capable of specific high affinity binding to promoter.
•This is followed by the binding of the other transcriptional factors (TFII A B, F, E and H) and RNA polymerase II.
•Preinitiation complex (PIC) is now formed of the TATA, RNA polymerase II, and the transcriptional factors.

sections.heading:
2 Initiation
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › C STEPS OF TRANSCRIPTION
sections.text:
•TFIIH has a helicase activity that separates the two strands of DNA for initiation.
•Also, it activates RNA polymerase II.
•This is followed by the release of TFII A, B, E & H.
•RNA polymerase II-TFIIF complex leaves the promoter region and moves towards the +1 nucleotide (Transcription start site).

sections.heading:
3 Elongation
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › C STEPS OF TRANSCRIPTION
sections.text:
•RNA polymerase II -TFIIF complex starts to synthesize a complementary transcript of the template DNA strand using ribonucleoside triphosphates (ATP, GTP, CTP and UTP) as substrates and releases pyrophosphate each time a nucleoside monophosphate is added to the growing chain.
•The process of elongation of the RNA chain continues until a termination signal is reached.

sections.heading:
4 Termination
02 RNA SYNTHESIS (TRANSCRIPTION) › C STEPS OF TRANSCRIPTION
sections.text: •Transcription is terminated when RNA polymerase II reaches a special termination sequence on the template strand of DNA

sections.heading: 03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA
sections.text:
•Messenger RNA is synthesized as a primary transcript (Immature) known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
•In the nucleus, post transcriptional modifications occur including capping, polyadenylation, splicing and mRNA editing.
•The mature functioning mRNA then combines with a protein to form mRNA-protein complex, which comes out through a nuclear pore to the cytoplasm.

sections.heading:
A CAPPING AT 5`END
03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA
sections.text:
•Methyl-guanosine cap is added at the 5`end
•Importance of capping:
▪It stabilizes the mRNA and protects it against the attack by ribonucleases.
▪It facilitates protein synthesis through helping the transport of mRNA to the cytoplasm and allows its recognition by the ribosomes (see later).

sections.heading:
B POLYADENYLATION AT 3` END
03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA
sections.text:
•Poly (A) polymerase (PAP) is responsible for the addition of poly(A) tail (Up to 200 adenine residues) at the 3`end of pre-mRNA.
•Importance of polyadenylation:
▪It stabilizes the mRNA and protects it against the attack by ribonucleases.
▪The length of poly (A) tail determines the half-life time of mRNA.
▪It increases the efficiency of protein synthesis through binding with specific poly A tail-binding proteins.

sections.heading:
C SPLICING
03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA
sections.text:
•In the primary RNA transcript, parts of mRNA do not code for amino acids.
•These sequences are known as introns.
•They lie between amino acid coding regions known as exons.
•Splicing removes introns (Non-expressed regions) & joins exons (Expressed regions) to form functional mRNA.
•Splicing requires a spliceosome which is small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) formed of special proteins and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs).

sections.heading:
Biomedical correlations
03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA › C SPLICING
sections.text:
•Systemic Lupus erythematosus (SLE):
▪An autoimmune disease characterized by autoantibodies against many cellular components.
▪Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) are one of the targets of these antibodies.
•Alternative splicing:
▪The primary transcript of some genes may be spliced differently to yield different proteins from the same gene.
▪This explains why the estimated number of proteins much exceeds the number of genes (e.g., antibody genes).

sections.heading:
D mRNA EDITING
03 POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS OF mRNA
sections.text:
•Coding information of mRNA can be changed by RNA editing.
•For example:
▪In the liver: the single apolipoprotein gene (Apo-B gene) is transcribed into an mRNA that directs the synthesis of apoB-100protein (100-kDa).
▪In the intestine: the same gene directs the synthesis of a primary transcript, then by the action of a cytidine deaminase, a CAA codon in mRNA is converted to UAA which is a termination codon.
▪ApoB-48 protein (48-kDa) is the result of translating this edited form of mRNA.
▪ApoB-100 and ApoB-48 proteins have different functions.

sections.heading:
A GENETIC CODE
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION)
sections.text:
•It is the nucleotide sequence of mRNA representing the code words for amino acids.
•Since the code words on mRNA originate from DNA genes, they are called «Genetic code».
•Each 3 successive nitrogenous bases in mRNA represents a codon.
•Since each codon is formed of 3 of the 4 bases (U, C, A, G), therefore there are 43=64 possible codons as follows:
▪One codon acts as initiation codon for protein synthesis i.e. AUG.
▪Three codons (UAA, UAG or UGA) do not code for any amino acid, and they are called termination codons (stop codons).
▪The remaining codons code for amino acids.

•Characteristics of genetic code
▪Specificity: A particular codon always codes for only one amino acid, e.g., UUU codes only for phenylalanine.
▪Degeneracy: An amino acid may be coded by more than one codon known as synonym codons (phenylalanine is coded by two synonym codons).
▪Universality: Genetic code is nearly universal (same in all organisms).
▪Reading frame: the codons are read from specific starting point (initiating codon) on the mRNA as a continuous uninterrupted sequence of bases taken 3 at a time.

sections.heading:
B CODON RECOGNITION BY tRNA
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION)
sections.text:
•Correct pairing of the codon of the mRNA with the anticodon of the tRNA is essential for accurate translation.
•Some tRNAs recognize more than one codon for a given amino acid.
•For a given codon on mRNA, an anti-codon is present on tRNA.
•Codon and anti-codon always read from 5` to 3` direction.
•Moreover, codon and anticodon are antiparallel and complementary in base composition. They interact with each other through base pairing.

sections.heading:
CC WOBBLE HYPOTHESIS
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION)
sections.text:
•The mechanism by which tRNAs can recognize more than one codon for a specific amino acid is described by the “Wobble” hypothesis.
•The first two nucleotides in the codon are essential, the third nucleotide is flexible, i.e., even if the third nucleotide is changed, that codon may indicate the same amino acid.
•Thus, the base pairing of the third nucleotide of codon with the first nucleotide of anti-codon is less specific.

•Translation is a process by which a cell makes protein using genetic information carried on mRNA.
•This process requires:
▪All three classes of RNA :
▫The mRNA which is the template for the correct addition of individual amino acids during synthesis of protein.
▫The tRNAs carry activated amino acids (in the form of aminoacyl-tRNA) into the ribosomes.
▫The ribosomes are associated with the mRNA and contain peptidyl transferase activity to catalyze peptide bond formation.
▪Amino acids: activated and carried on tRNA
▪A source of energy (ATP and GTP)
▪Different protein factors required for the process to be completed.

sections.heading:
A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION)
sections.text:
•Rough endoplasmic reticulum is the site of formation of proteins in eukaryotes.
•After formation of aminoacyl-tRNA, the mechanism of translation involves three main phases: initiation, elongation, and termination.

sections.heading:
1 Formation of Aminoacyl-tRNA
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION) › A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•In the cytosol, the 20 different amino acids are carried on their corresponding tRNAs by 20 different amino-acyl-tRNA synthetases
•Each of which is specific for one amino acid and its corresponding tRNA.
•The formation of aminoacyl-tRNA occurs in two steps:
▪First, is the formation of enzyme-AMP-amino acid complex, with hydrolysis of ATP into AMP and PPi.
▪Second, is formation of aminoacyl-tRNA complex & release of the enzyme & AMP.
•Aminoacyl-tRNA is said to be “Charged tRNA".

sections.heading:
2 Synthesis of the Polypeptide Chain in Eukaryotes
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION) › A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS
sections.text:
•The process of translation is classified into three main phases:
▪Initiation
▪Elongation
▪Termination.
•Special protein factors for initiation (initiation factors, IFs), elongation (EFs) and termination (release factors) are required for each stage respectively.

sections.heading:
A. Initiation:
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION) › A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS › 2 Synthesis of the Polypeptide Chain in Eukaryotes
sections.text:
•It involves the assembly of the components of protein synthesis at the initiation codon.
•IF-4 binds to 5`- cap of mRNA.
•IF-4 facilitates the binding of mRNA to 40S ribosomal subunit.
•The 40S subunit moves on the mRNA to reach the first codon (AUG).
•The initiating methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) becomes bound to the AUG start codon on the mRNA.
•The 60S subunit of the ribosome binds to the 40S subunit forming the completed 80S initiation complex, with release of IF-4.
•Two important binding sites on 80S ribosome are the P and A sites.
▪The peptidyl site (P site): It is the site on the ribosome where the initiator methionine tRNA (Met-tRNAi) initially binds.
▪The aminoacyl site (A site): It binds the new coming tRNA molecule carrying an activated amino acid.
•At the end of initiation, met-tRNAi is on the P-site, while the A-site remains vacant and ready to accept the next aminoacyl-tRNA during elongation.

sections.heading:
B. Elongation:
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION) › A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS › 2 Synthesis of the Polypeptide Chain in Eukaryotes
sections.text:
•Elongation is a 3-step cycle that is repeated for each amino acid added to the protein after the initiator methionine.
•During elongation, the ribosome moves from the 5ˋ to 3ˋdirection along the mRNA, synthesizing the protein from amino to carboxyl terminus.
•The 3 steps are:
▪Binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A-site:
▫The charged tRNA binds to the A-site.
▫The aminoacyl-tRNA is determined by the mRNA codon aligned with the A-site.
▪Peptide bond formation:
▫Peptidyl transferase, an enzyme which is part of the 60S subunit, forms the peptide bond between the amino group of the new aminoacyl-tRNA in the A-site with carboxylic group of the peptidyl chain carried by tRNA occupying the P-site.
▫This results in attachment of the growing peptide to tRNA in the A-site (i.e., now peptidyl-tRNA is in the A-site).
▪Translocation:
▫The ribosome moves exactly 3 nucleotides (One codon) along the mRNA.
▫This moves the growing peptidyl-tRNA from A-site to the P-site.
▫Which frees the A-site to accept a new aminoacyl-tRNA according to the next codon present.
▫The new cycle of elongation restarts.
▫The process of polypeptide chain synthesis continues until

termination codon is reached.

sections.heading:
C. Termination
04 PROTEIN SYNTHESIS (TRANSLATION) › A STEPS OF PROTEIN SYNTHESIS › 2 Synthesis of the Polypeptide Chain in Eukaryotes
sections.text:
•The elongation steps are repeated until a termination (Stop) codon appears in the A-site of the ribosome.
•Since there is no tRNA with anticodon that can pair with the stop codon, a releasing factor binds to the ribosome instead, causing peptidyl transferase to hydrolyze the bond between the peptide chain and tRNA.
•The mRNA, ribosome, tRNA and the different protein factors can all be reused for additional protein synthesis

•Many ribosomes can work on the same mRNA molecule
•These aggregates are called polyribosomes or polysomes and are attached to the wall of the endoplasmic reticulum to form rough ER.
•In such cases each ribosome is about 80-100 nucleotide apart on mRNA.

sections.heading: 05 POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS
sections.text:
•Most proteins, which emerge from ribosomes, are biologically inactive.
•Post-translational modifications convert them into functional proteins.
•Usually, protein may attain proper conformation by the time it is released from the ribosome.
•Post-translational modifications include mainly the following:

sections.heading:
A TRIMMING
05 POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS
sections.text:
•Many proteins secreted from cell are initially made as large, precursor molecules that are not functionally active.
•Portions of the protein chain must be removed by specialized endoproteases, which results in the release of an active molecule.
•For example:
▪Insulin is formed as pre-proinsulin which is converted to proinsulin then to insulin.
▪Zymogens are inactive precursors of secreted enzymes, e.g., trypsinogen becomes activated to trypsin in the small intestine.

sections.heading:
B COVALENTMODIFICATION
05 POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS
sections.text:
•Amino acid residues within the peptide chain can be modified enzymatically
•Modification is to achieve one or more of the following functions:
▪Alter the activity or stability of the proteins.
▪Direct it to a subcellular compartment.
▪Prepare it for secretion from the cell.
•Amino acid residues are modified enzymatically by the addition of various types of functional groups.
•For example:
▪Phosphorylation / Dephosphorylation:
▫The addition and removal of phosphate groups (Which bind covalently to serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues)
▫Serve to regulate the activity of many proteins (e.g., the enzymes of glycogen metabolism and regulators of gene transcription).
▪Glycosylation:
▫The addition of carbohydrate groups is a common modification that occurs mainly on proteins that are destined to be secreted or incorporated into lysosomes or cellular membranes.
▪Acetylation or methylation:
▫The N-terminal amino acid is sometimes acetylated or methylated.
▫These changes alter the charge on the protein
▫E.g., chromatin remodeling by histone acetylation (explained later).
▪Hydroxylation:
▫In collagen, hydroxylation of prolyl & lysyl residues leads to stabilization of protein.
▪Carboxylation:
▫Formation of γ-carboxyglutamate of some blood coagulation proteins allows them to bind Ca+2, a step occurs in clot formation.

sections.heading: 06 GENE MUTATIONS
sections.text:
•Mutations are defined as permanent changes in a DNA sequence.
•Causes of Mutations:

sections.heading:
A ERRORS IN REPLICATION
06 GENE MUTATIONS
sections.text: •If a non-complementary base to the template base is added during replication, this leads to mutation if the error is not repaired.

sections.heading:
1 Chemical mutagens
06 GENE MUTATIONS › B DAMAGE OF THE NUCLEOTIDES OF DNA
sections.text: •Chemical mutagens are chemicals inhaled or absorbed from the environment that cause mutations. e.g., cigarette smoke contains carcinogens.

sections.heading:
2 Irradiation
06 GENE MUTATIONS › B DAMAGE OF THE NUCLEOTIDES OF DNA
sections.text: •Ultraviolet light (UV) or ionizing radiation (x-rays and gamma rays) can alter the structure of DNA.

sections.heading:
3 Oxidative damage
06 GENE MUTATIONS › B DAMAGE OF THE NUCLEOTIDES OF DNA
sections.text:
•Oxidative DNA damage is implicated in several diseases.
•Diseases range from neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease to cancer.
•Also, DNA oxidative damage has been shown to play a part in the aging process.

Regardless of the method of formation, there are only limited types of gene mutations.

sections.heading:
A BASE SUBSTITUTION (POINT MUTATIONS)
06 GENE MUTATIONS
sections.text:
•Base substitutions are the most common type of mutation.
•They may occur in the coding region of a gene
•They can produce one of the following effects: Missense, nonsense, or silent mutation.

sections.heading:
1 Missense mutation
06 GENE MUTATIONS › A BASE SUBSTITUTION (POINT MUTATIONS)
sections.text:
•Leads to a changed codon & results in an amino acid change in protein product of it.
•Depending on the amino acid changed, missense mutations can have either no effect or very serious changes e.g., sickle cell anemia.

sections.heading:
2 Nonsense mutation
06 GENE MUTATIONS › A BASE SUBSTITUTION (POINT MUTATIONS)
sections.text:
•Leads to the conversion of an amino acid codon to a stop or non-sense codon.
•Translation of the mRNA from that gene is prematurely terminated and the protein product is usually non-functional e.g., thalassemia.

sections.heading:
3 Silent mutation
06 GENE MUTATIONS › A BASE SUBSTITUTION (POINT MUTATIONS)
sections.text: •Leads to formation of a synonym codon that codes for the same amino acid and no change occurs in the amino acid sequence of the gene products.

sections.heading:
B DELETION OR INSERTION OF ONE OR MORE BASES
06 GENE MUTATIONS
sections.text: •This type includes:

sections.heading:
1 Frameshift mutation:
06 GENE MUTATIONS › B DELETION OR INSERTION OF ONE OR MORE BASES
sections.text:
•It occurs if a deletion or insertion of bases in a gene is not a multiple of three e.g., one or two bases.
•The reading frame of the translated mRNA is changed.
•This usually results in the production of a nonfunctional gene product.

sections.heading:
2 Deletion or insertion of three or multiple of three bases:
06 GENE MUTATIONS › B DELETION OR INSERTION OF ONE OR MORE BASES
sections.text:
•This produces no changes in the reading frame and only a deletion or insertion of one or more amino acids from the encoded protein.
•Such mutation is less severe than the frameshift mutation.

sections.heading: IN THIS CHAPTER — Controlling when and how genes are expressed
sections.text:
01 Introduction to Regulation of Gene Expression
02 Regulation of Eukaryotic Gene Expression

sections.heading: 01 INTRODUCTION TO REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text:
•The process of gene expression needs to be strictly regulated to ensure that cells produce the correct number of proteins when they need them.
•Any disruption to this regulation can lead to serious consequences.
•There are two types of genes:
▪Unregulated genes (Constitutive or housekeeping):
▸These genes are continually expressed at fixed rate & are not subjected to regulation
▸They encode proteins that are continuously required for basic cellular functions, such as β-actin gene.
▪Regulated genes:
▸These genes represent the majority and are expressed only under certain conditions.
▸They encode proteins only when they are required, such as globin genes.

sections.heading: 02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text: •Regulation of gene expression occurs at multiple levels, mainly at level of transcription.

sections.heading:
1 Epigenetic Mechanisms
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION › A PRE-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
sections.text:
•Epigenetic means “Around the gene”, it refers to the changes that occur to the DNA and the histone proteins.
•These changes do not alter the sequence of DNA.
▸DNA Methylation:
▪Methylation of a specific cytosine to form 5`methylcytosine by DNA methyltransferase.
▪The target cytosine is usually located next to a guanine residue, forming a CpG island, which is often near or in the promoter region of a gene.
▪It is associated with the silencing of the activities of certain genes.
▪It is a mechanism for regulating gene expression during cell differentiation, particularly in fetal development.
▪Demethylation reverses the process.

▸Chromatin Remodeling
▪The cellular genome is packaged together with histones into chromatin structures.
▪Activation of a gene for transcription requires changes in the state of the chromatin, to make the desired region accessible to RNAP and other proteins (e.g., transcriptional factors).
▪This is called chromatin remodeling.
▪This occurs through different mechanisms, for example, histone acetylation.
▪Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) transfer an acetyl group from acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) to lysine residues in the tail of the histone octamer.
▪This reaction removes a positive charge from the ε-amino group of the lysine, thereby reducing the electrostatic interactions between the histones and the negatively charged DNA.
▪This makes it easier for DNA to unwind from the histones with simultaneous activation of the gene and initiation of its transcription.
▪The acetyl groups can be removed by histone deacetylases (HDACs) to form inactive chromatin.

sections.heading:
2 Epigenetic Mechanisms
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION › A PRE-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
sections.text:
•A change in the number of copies of a gene can affect amount of gene product produced
•This include:
▪Gene amplification (Increase the number): This is seen in response to certain chemotherapeutic drugs such as methotrexate, an inhibitor of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), required for the synthesis of DNA.
▪Malignant cells can develop resistance to methotrexate by amplification of the gene for this enzyme.
▪Gene diminution (Decrease the number): This occurs during development of RBCs as all genes disappear during maturation.

sections.heading:
3 Gene Rearrangement
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION › A PRE-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
sections.text:
•Heavy & light chains of Igs are encoded by several hundred gene segments.
•Their rearrangement or recombination allows generation of several million different immunoglobulins, providing the antibody diversity needed for the recognition of an enormous number of antigens.

sections.heading:
B TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text: •Regulation of gene expression at the level of transcription occurs through interaction between cis- and trans-acting elements.

sections.heading:
1 Cis-acting elements
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION › B TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
sections.text:
•These are DNA regulatory sequences flanking a gene.
•They are usually embedded in the non-coding regions of the genome.
•They influence expression of genes only on the same chromosome.
•The interaction between these DNA segments & regulatory molecules, such as transcription factors, can induce or repress the transcriptional machinery, influencing the kinds and amounts of products.
•Cis- acting elements include:
1Promoter :
▪Two types of sequence elements are present in promoter
▪The TATA box & the CAAT box & GC box regions (Discussed in transcription).
2Enhancers and silencers:
▪Enhancers are special elements in DNA → Facilitate initiation of transcription.
▪They act by binding certain proteins that facilitate the binding of transcription factors to the promoter.
▪However, they can be close to or thousands of base pairs away from promoter (Upstream or downstream) & they can occur on either strand of DNA.
▪Silencers are special elements in DNA that inhibit initiation of transcription.
▪They act by binding certain proteins that produce inhibition of transcription.
3Hormone-Response Elements:
▪These are elements in DNA that permit hormones to regulate transcription
▪When the hormone receptor complex binds the specific element in DNA
▪e.g., steroid and thyroid hormones.

sections.heading:
2 Trans-acting elements
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION › B TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
sections.text:
•They are the regulatory molecules which can diffuse from their site of synthesis in the cell to the DNA-binding site.
•For example:
▪Trans-acting molecule is transcribed from a gene on chromosome 11 and regulates another gene on chromosome 6.

sections.heading:
C POST-TRANSCRIPTIONALREGULATION
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text:
•Capping, poly-A tailing, and splicing:
▪Discussed in transcription.
•miRNAs:
▪They are non-coding RNAs that reduce expression of the target mRNA either by inducing its degradation or blocking its translation.

sections.heading:
D TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text:
•Phosphorylation of some IFs blocks protein synthesis.
•They are phosphorylated by protein kinases that are activated when the cell is under stress and when energy utilization for protein synthesis is deleterious e.g. starvation.

sections.heading:
E POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION OF PROTEINS
02 REGULATION OF EUKARYOTIC GENE EXPRESSION
sections.text:

2Covalent Modification

sections.heading: 01 CELL CYCLE
sections.text: Cell cycle is a series of events that take place in a cell as it grows & divides into 2 daughter cells

sections.heading:
A PHASES OF CELL CYCLE
01 CELL CYCLE
sections.text:
•The cell cycle is divided into two main phases: the mitotic phase (M) & the interphase (I)
•Interphase is further divided into three phases (G1, S and G2).
•G1: Growth
•S: Synthesis of DNA
•G2: Growth & preparation for mitosis
•M: Mitosis
•G0: Resting

•The cell spends most of its time in the interphase, during which it grows, replicates its chromosomes, and prepares itself for cell division.
•The cell then leaves the interphase, undergoes mitosis, and completes its division.
•G1 phase:
▪The stage where the cell grows by increasing in size, and checks DNA to repair any damage by replication.
•S phase:
▪The stage where the cell replicates its DNA (S stands for synthesis of DNA).
•G2 phase:
▪The stage where the cell grows more and prepares itself to divide.
•M phase:
▪The stage of mitosis where the cell separates the 2 copies of the genetic material into two identical daughter cells.
•G0 phase:
▪After passing through mitosis and into G1, the cell either continues through another division or stops dividing (entering a quiescent phase G0).
▪In G0, the cell is said to be in the resting state performing its function without dividing.
▪G0 is a permanent state for some cells, e.g., most adult neuronal cells.

sections.heading:
B REGULATION OF CELL CYCLE
01 CELL CYCLE
sections.text:
•The cell cycle is mainly controlled by:
▪Regulatory proteins (Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases)
▪Checkpoints at different stages
•The cell cycle is controlled by a group of regulatory proteins called:
▪Cyclins and Cyclin Dependent Kinases (CDK).
•The cell cycle is initiated by binding of a growth factor to a growth factor receptor on the plasma membrane of the cell.
•This mediates an intracellular signaling cascade that induces cyclins genes.
•Cyclins complex with and activate certain CDKs that produce regulatory effects essential for the passage of the cell from one phase to another.
•There are at least 10 different cyclins (Designated A, B, and so forth) & at least 8 CDKs
•They act in various combinations at specific points in the cell cycle as follows:
▪Progression past restriction point at G1/S boundary.
▪Initiation of DNA synthesis in early S phase.
▪Transition from G2 to M phase.

sections.heading:
Restriction point
01 CELL CYCLE › B REGULATION OF CELL CYCLE
sections.text:
•The restriction point (R) is located at the late G1 stage.
•The cells that pass through the R point will enter the S phase and complete the entire cycle independently on the presence of the growth factors.

sections.heading:
2 Cell Cycle Checkpoints
01 CELL CYCLE › B REGULATION OF CELL CYCLE
sections.text:
•There are three check points to ensure that DNA and chromosomal structure are intact before the cell cycle is completed as explained by the following diagram.

•If there is a defect in any of the cell cycle regulatory proteins or checkpoints, or if the cell suffers from irreparable damage to DNA prior to S phase, it may destroy itself in response to programmed steps.
•This is called “apoptosis”.

sections.heading: 02 APOPTOSIS
sections.text:
•Apoptosis is programmed genetically directed cell death (physiological cell suicide program).
•Many cells can precisely control the time of their own death by apoptosis (app›-a-toe›-sis from the Greek for «dropping off,» as in leaves dropping in the fall).

sections.heading:
A BIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE
02 APOPTOSIS
sections.text:
•Eliminating individual cells whose survival would be harmful to the organism.
•When a cell is damaged beyond repair, infected with a virus, experiencing starvation or under the effects of ionizing radiation or toxins (causing irreparable damage to DNA), apoptosis is stimulated.
•Development: Apoptosis is used during development of the embryo.
•Homeostasis: In normal, healthy adults, the number of cells is kept relatively constant owing to a balance between cell division and cell death.
•If the equilibrium is disturbed, then abnormal growth & tumors or abnormal cell loss can result.
There are two main pathways for apoptosis:

sections.heading:
1 Extrinsic pathway
02 APOPTOSIS › B MECHANISMS OF APOPTOSIS
sections.text:
•It is initiated through binding of a certain ligand to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) or FAS receptors.
•This binding leads to activation of several caspases (Caspases are intracellular cysteine proteases).
•Activated Caspases activate caspase-activated DNase (CADase)
•The enzyme that cuts genomic DNA between nucleosomes generating DNA fragments of approximately 200 bp or its multiples.
•Responsible for characteristic DNA ladder pattern observed after DNA electrophoresis.

sections.heading:
2 Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway
02 APOPTOSIS › B MECHANISMS OF APOPTOSIS
sections.text:
•It is used extensively in response to different forms of cellular stress.
•These stressors promote the release of cytochrome C from mitochondria into cytosol.
•Released cytochrome C activates caspases, leading to activation of CADase and induction of the apoptotic process.
•Regulation of intrinsic pathway:
▪Bcl2- family members are important regulators of the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway. These members include two main functional groups:
▪Anti-apoptotic modulators: (Bcl2-, Bcl-x, etc.) possess anti-apoptotic activity.
▪Apoptotic modulators: (Bax, Bak, Bok) exert their apoptosis-modulating effects by controlling the release of cytochrome c from mitochondria to cytosol.
▪Under physiological conditions, there is balance between the two groups.

sections.heading:
Apoptosis and Cancer
02 APOPTOSIS › B MECHANISMS OF APOPTOSIS › 2 Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway
sections.text: •Cancer arises when the homeostatic balance between cell division and apoptosis is altered. Decreased apoptosis in cancer cells may result from altered expression of apoptosis regulatory proteins.

sections.heading: 03 TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES
sections.text:
•Tumor suppressor genes encode proteins that have at least one of these functions:
▪Proteins that are activated in response to DNA damage, e.g. p53.
▪Proteins that inhibit progression through a specific stage of the cell cycle and give it time to repair, e.g. p21.
▪Proteins that promote apoptosis e.g. protein Bax.
▪DNA repair enzymes: They are termed anti-oncogenes; & their mutations remove certain control on growth & proliferation which play a major role in the development of cancer.

sections.heading:
B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
03 TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES
sections.text:
•This gene encodes a nuclear phosphoprotein called p53.
•It has a molecular weight of 53 kDa.
•p53 is called the “Molecular Policeman” or “Guardian of the Genome”.
•In Moderate DNA Damage:
▪Certain protein kinases phosphorylate p53 and make it active.
▪Active phosphorylated p53 serves as a transcription factor that induces the synthesis of the protein p21.
▪Protein p21 inhibits the protein kinase activity of a specific CDK-cyclin complex, & the cell cycle is arrested in Gl.
▪This gives the cell time to repair its DNA before entering the S phase,
▪thereby avoiding the potentially disastrous transfer of a defective genome to one or both daughter cells.
•In Severe DNA Damage:
▪Certain protein kinases phosphorylate p53 and make it active.
▪Active phosphorylated p53 induces Bax gene transcription.
▪Bax protein triggers apoptosis. So, this will lead to the death of the cell.

sections.heading:
Biomedical Correlation
03 TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES › B HETEROPOLYSACCHARIDES
sections.text:
•Mutation in the p53 gene leads to genomic instability.
•decreased apoptosis and leads to cancer.
•About 50% of human cancers have a mutated p53 gene.
•Aflatoxin (Fungal toxin) causes mutation of p53 and may lead to hepatic cancer.
•Benzopyrene (Smoking) causes mutation of p53 and may lead to lung cancer.
